lectures.name: Orbital Anatomy
lectures.title: Orbital anatomy
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ "LR6, SO4, the rest 3": a third nerve palsy leaves the eye down and out with ptosis, a fourth nerve palsy up and in, and a sixth nerve palsy cannot look outward. The floor breaks in a blowout fracture (teardrop sign). Ciliary body makes aqueous humor, Schlemm's canal drains it - blocked drainage is glaucoma. Pupil constrictor = parasympathetic (III); dilator = sympathetic. A pupil-involving third nerve palsy suggests compression. Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden blindness, cherry-red spot.

blocks.html: Every orbital symptom points to a structure: know which walls break, where the eye's fluid is made and drained, and which nerve moves each muscle - then a blowout, a high-pressure eye, a droopy lid or a wandering eye tells you what is damaged.
1. The bony orbit

blocks.lead: A cone of bone that holds the eye, which sits mostly in fat.
rows: Frontal bone (+ lesser wing of the sphenoid)
Zygomatic bone + greater wing of the sphenoid
Maxilla (+ small parts of zygomatic and palatine)

blocks.html: (sources differ: the note puts the ethmoid at the back of the orbit and the lacrimal bone at the back-and-middle; the upper-year notes put both in the medial wall - check the slides)

• Blowout fracture: a blow to the eye pushes out the weak floor or medial wall
    • floor fracture: orbital fat herniates into the maxillary sinus → "teardrop sign" on imaging

rows: Optic nerve (cranial nerve II) + ophthalmic artery
Superior orbital fissure (between the two sphenoid wings)
Cranial nerves III, IV, VI · branches of the ophthalmic nerve (V1: lacrimal, frontal, nasociliary) · superior and inferior ophthalmic veins
Infraorbital branch of the maxillary nerve (V2) + infraorbital artery

blocks.cap: The seven bones of the orbit with the optic canal and the superior and inferior orbital fissures

blocks.html: 2. The eyeball: layers and chambers

• Outer (fibrous) layer
    • Sclera = tough white coat, where the extraocular muscles insert · cornea = its clear front, where light enters
  • Middle (vascular) layer
    • Choroid = vessels + pigment that stops light scattering
    • Ciliary body = muscle that changes lens shape + processes that make aqueous humor
    • Iris = coloured ring around the pupil (see section 3)
  • Inner layer: retina = rods and cones
    • Optic disc = where the optic nerve leaves: no photoreceptors → blind spot
    • Macula with the fovea in its centre = sharpest vision
  • Chambers
    • anterior (cornea to iris) and posterior (iris to lens) chambers: watery aqueous humor
    • vitreous chamber: gel-like vitreous humor that holds the retina in place
  • Aqueous flow: ciliary body → posterior chamber → through the pupil → anterior chamber → drained at the angle into Schlemm's canal → veins
    • drainage blocked → ↑ pressure inside the eye = glaucoma → presses on the retina → blindness if untreated
  • Lens: hung from the ciliary body by suspensory ligaments
    • ciliary muscle contracts → ligaments slacken → lens rounds up for near vision · lost with age (presbyopia, by about 45)
    • clouded lens = cataracts (damaged, misfolded lens proteins, e.g. from sunlight)

blocks.cap: Layers of the eyeball: sclera, choroid and retina; cornea, iris, ciliary body, lens and conjunctiva

blocks.html: 3. Iris and pupil

rows: Parasympathetic: cranial nerve III → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves
Sympathetic: superior cervical ganglion → long ciliary nerves

blocks.html: 4. Eyelid, conjunctiva and tears

• Conjunctiva: palpebral part lines the lid, bulbar part covers the eye (not the cornea) → together a conjunctival sac · secretes lubricating mucus
    • infection = conjunctivitis (pink eye)
  • Lacrimal gland (upper outer orbit) makes tears
    • parasympathetic supply from the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) - via the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion, reaching the gland in the lacrimal branch of V1
  • Tear drainage: blinking sweeps tears from lateral to medial → puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → nasal cavity (inferior meatus)
    • infected lacrimal sac = dacryocystitis
  • Tarsal glands (in the lid): oil that keeps tears on the cornea · clogged or infected = stye (warm compresses; minor surgery if needed)
  • Levator palpebrae superioris lifts the lid: skeletal fibres (cranial nerve III, voluntary) + smooth fibres (sympathetic, widen the eyes in danger)
    • so ptosis (droopy lid) comes from either a third nerve palsy or Horner's syndrome
5. Extraocular muscles

rows: IV (trochlear) - runs through a pulley, the trochlea
Up and out - the only one that does not start at the back of the orbit (starts on the medial floor)

blocks.html:
• The superior and inferior recti also pull the eye inward because the orbit points outward at an angle to the line of sight
  • "LR6, SO4, the rest 3"

blocks.alt: extraocular muscles anterior view - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The extraocular muscles seen from the front: the four recti and two obliques around the eyeball

blocks.html: 6. Nerves and palsies

• Optic nerve (II) = vision · runs through the optic canal in a sheath of meninges with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
  • III, IV, VI enter through the superior orbital fissure · ophthalmic nerve (V1) = sensation from the orbit, upper lid and conjunctiva
  • At rest the muscles balance each other, so a palsy lets the unopposed muscles pull the eye → double vision (diplopia)

rows: Down and out (lateral rectus + superior oblique unopposed)
Ptosis · may have a large pupil - pupil fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so compression (e.g. aneurysm) takes the pupil; a pupil-sparing palsy suggests ischemia (e.g. diabetes)
Head tilt · often trauma or congenital - the least worrying
Turns the head toward the bad side to stop double vision · can be the first sign of ↑ intracranial pressure (long course from the brainstem)
Small pupil, mild ptosis, no sweating - sympathetic supply lost

blocks.html: 7. Blood supply

• Ophthalmic artery = first branch of the internal carotid inside the skull · enters through the optic canal
    • central retinal artery runs inside the optic nerve to the retina → occlusion = sudden, complete blindness · pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula
  • Veins: superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus · inferior ophthalmic vein → pterygoid plexus

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of Vision
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of vision
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Nasal retinal fibres cross at the chiasm: a chiasm lesion gives bitemporal hemianopia; anything behind the chiasm gives a homonymous hemianopia on the opposite side. Near vision = ciliary muscle contracts, lens rounds. Fovea = cones only, sharpest vision; periphery = rods, dim light. Glaucoma takes the periphery first, macular degeneration the centre, cataract blurs everything. Light reflex: in via II, out via III, both pupils constrict.

blocks.html: The lens focuses light, the retina turns it into signals, and the pathway sorts those signals by visual field on the way to the occipital cortex - so the shape of a field defect tells you where the lesion is.
1. Focusing the image: accommodation
• The lens bends light to land a sharp, upside-down image on the retina; it changes shape to keep the target in focus (accommodation)

• Ageing: the lens stiffens and stays too flat → near objects blur → reading glasses (presbyopia)
  • Eyeball shape off: can't see far (myopia) → concave lens · can't see near (hyperopia) → convex lens

blocks.cap: Accommodation: a rounder lens focuses a near target, a flatter lens a far one

blocks.html: 2. Pupillary light reflex

• Bright light → pupil constricts → protects the photoreceptors from saturating and sharpens the image
  • Light in one eye constricts both pupils (consensual) - if not, something is wrong with the nerves or brainstem
  • In: optic nerve (cranial nerve II) → Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain → out: parasympathetic fibres in the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) → ciliary ganglion → constrictor muscle
  • A subcortical reflex - tests II, III and the midbrain, not the visual cortex

blocks.alt: pupillary light reflex pathway - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The pupillary light reflex: retina and optic nerve to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, back out via nerve III and the ciliary ganglion to both pupils

blocks.html: 3. The retina

• Light passes through every layer to reach the photoreceptors at the back
  • Five cell types: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → retinal ganglion cells (the only ones that fire action potentials; their ~1 million axons form the optic nerve) · horizontal and amacrine cells link neighbours sideways
  • Phototransduction: light closes sodium channels → the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes → releases less transmitter · darkness does the opposite

rows: Low - many converge on one ganglion cell (large receptive field)

blocks.html:
• Optic disc = blind spot: no photoreceptors where the axons leave · lies nasal to the fovea, so the blind spot is in the temporal visual field · the brain fills it in
  • Reading in dim light is hard: you rely on rods, which are not in the fovea
  • Ganglion cells: P cells (~90%, small fields, colour and fine detail, fed by cones) and M cells (large fields, motion and flicker, fed by rods) · their centre-surround fields pick out edges
  • Colour blindness: ~8% of males (X-linked), ~0.5% of females · red-green is the usual form
4. Diseases of the eye

rows: ↑ pressure in the eye squeezes ganglion-cell axons
Fatty deposits or abnormal new vessels under the macula distort the retina

blocks.html: 5. Central visual pathway and lesions

• The image is reversed: the right visual field lands on the left half of each retina
  • Optic nerve (one eye, both halves of its field) → optic chiasm: fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross (they see the temporal field) → optic tract carries the opposite visual hemifield from both eyes
    • (sources differ: the note says fibres from the "nasal visual field" cross; the upper-year notes say the nasal retina - which sees the temporal field - and the note's own worked example agrees with that - check the slides)
  • ~90% → lateral geniculate nucleus (thalamus) → optic radiations → primary visual cortex (V1) around the calcarine sulcus, occipital lobe
  • ~10% → midbrain: superior colliculus (orienting) · Edinger-Westphal nucleus (pupillary light reflex)

rows: Homonymous hemianopia - the same half in both eyes, opposite the lesion

blocks.alt: visual hemifields to optic nerves chiasm and tracts - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Each visual hemifield reaches both eyes; after the chiasm, the left field travels in the right optic tract and the right field in the left

blocks.html: • Beyond V1: a dorsal "where/action" stream to the parietal lobe (damage → can't guide reaching by sight, optic ataxia) and a ventral "what" stream to the temporal lobe (damage → can't recognise objects, visual agnosia, or faces, prosopagnosia)

lectures.name: Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon
lectures.title: Neuroanatomy of the brainstem, basal ganglia and diencephalon
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Direct pathway (D1) releases the thalamus = GO; indirect pathway (D2, through the external pallidus and subthalamic nucleus) inhibits it = NO-GO - lose nigral dopamine and you get Parkinson disease (too little GO); lose the striatum and you get Huntington chorea (too little NO-GO). Thalamus relays every sense but smell. Hypothalamus = visceral and endocrine control. Corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla. The cerebellum works on the same side of the body.

blocks.html: The structures at the core of the brain, and what each one does: the diencephalon relays and regulates, the basal ganglia pick which movement goes ahead, the brainstem carries the tracts and cranial nerve nuclei, and the cerebellum coordinates.
1. Diencephalon

blocks.lead: The grey-matter core of the forebrain, wrapped by the cerebral hemispheres.
rows: Centre of the brain · ~80% of the diencephalon
The relay: every sense except smell has a thalamic nucleus that sends to its primary cortex · organizes, amplifies or dampens signals · held under constant inhibition by the basal ganglia
Between the optic chiasm and the mammillary bodies · pituitary hangs below
Visceral control centre: autonomic system, temperature, hunger and thirst, sleep-wake, endocrine control, memory, behaviour, emotion
Secretes melatonin in low light (light input relayed from the suprachiasmatic nucleus) → circadian rhythm, sleep
Subthalamic nucleus - part of the basal ganglia circuit

blocks.html:
• Thalamic nuclei
    • relay: ventral posterior lateral (VPL) = body sensation · lateral geniculate = vision · medial geniculate = hearing
    • motor: ventral anterior (input from the globus pallidus) · ventral lateral (input from the cerebellum)
    • limbic and association: anterior (limbic) · medial dorsal (from the amygdala) · pulvinar (to the parietal cortex)
  • Hypothalamic zones: periventricular (hormone output - paraventricular and arcuate nuclei) · medial (limbic links) · lateral (dopamine and serotonin fibres passing through - the reward pathway)

blocks.cap: The thalamic nuclei: sensory relay, motor, limbic and higher-order groups

blocks.html: 2. Basal ganglia: the parts
Deep grey-matter nuclei that release the wanted movement and suppress the rest (also roles in cognition, learning and emotion).

• Striatum = the input: caudate nucleus (arches over the thalamus, beside the lateral ventricle) + putamen · the nucleus accumbens is the ventral striatum
  • Lentiform nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus
    • external globus pallidus (GPe) = the indirect pathway's relay · internal globus pallidus (GPi) = the output to the thalamus
  • Subthalamic nucleus - excites the internal globus pallidus in the indirect pathway
  • Substantia nigra (midbrain) - its dopamine neurons modulate the striatum · another part suppresses the superior colliculus to stop unwanted eye movements
  • Loop: cortex → striatum → globus pallidus → thalamus → motor cortex
3. Direct vs indirect pathway

blocks.lead: At rest the internal globus pallidus fires steadily and keeps the thalamus inhibited.
rows: Cortex → striatum ⊣ internal pallidus ⊣ thalamus → motor cortex
Cortex → striatum ⊣ external pallidus ⊣ subthalamic nucleus → internal pallidus ⊣ thalamus
Parkinson disease: nigral dopamine neurons lost → too little GO → bradykinesia
Huntington disease: caudate and putamen degenerate → too little NO-GO → chorea

blocks.html: (→ excites · ⊣ inhibits)

blocks.cap: Direct pathway: striatum inhibits the internal globus pallidus, releasing the thalamus to drive the motor cortex
Indirect pathway: through the external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, ending in more inhibition of the thalamus

blocks.html: 4. Brainstem

blocks.lead: Midbrain, pons and medulla: carries the tracts between brain and cord, holds the cranial nerve nuclei (III to XII), and runs heart rate, breathing, sleep and eating.
rows: Cerebral aqueduct ringed by periaqueductal grey (pain suppression) · red nucleus · substantia nigra
Bulge of pontine nuclei, with the corticospinal tract running through
Pontine nuclei relay the cortex to the opposite cerebellum (middle peduncle)
Pyramids (corticospinal) → pyramidal decussation at the bottom · olives (to the cerebellum)
Autonomic and breathing control near the midline

blocks.html:
• Fourth ventricle lies over the upper medulla and lower pons · the cord's central canal opens into it at the obex
  • Reticular formation: arousal, pain modulation, autonomic reflexes, movement · central pattern generators
  • Tracts passing through: up - spinothalamic, dorsal column-medial lemniscus, spinocerebellar · down - corticospinal, corticobulbar
  • Cranial nerve nuclei: sensory-only nerves (I, II, VIII) and motor-only nerves (III, IV, VI, XI, XII) have one nucleus each · mixed nerves (V, VII, IX, X) have several
  • Where III to XII leave: midbrain III-IV · pons V-VIII · medulla IX-XII (see 04 - Introduction to Neuroanatomy)
5. Cerebellum

• Posterior fossa, under the tentorium · grows out of the pons · cortex of folia, white matter, deep nuclei
  • Controls the same (ipsilateral) side of the body - unlike the motor cortex
  • Compares the planned movement with body position and ongoing movement, then corrects the cortex · motor memory
  • Somatotopy: vermis (midline) = trunk · paravermis = limbs
  • Peduncles: superior → midbrain · middle → pons · inferior → medulla

rows: Balance, vestibulo-ocular reflex, trunk and limb stability
Anterior lobe (note) · vermis + intermediate zone (upper-year notes)
Adjusts ongoing trunk and limb movement and tone

lectures.name: Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum
lectures.title: Neuroanatomy of the spinal tracts and cerebellum
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Dorsal columns cross in the medulla, spinothalamic fibres cross in the cord where they enter, and the lateral corticospinal tract crosses at the pyramids - so a one-sided cord lesion takes vibration, position and power on its own side but pain and temperature on the other. Spinocerebellar tracts end up on the same side. Gracilis = leg, cuneatus = arm. UMN facial weakness spares the forehead. Sensory = 3 neurons through the VPL; motor = 2 neurons, UMN and LMN.

blocks.html: Every tract question comes down to two facts: what it carries, and where it crosses. Put those together and a lesion's level and side tell you which modalities go, and on which side.
1. How the pathways are built

• Ascending (sensory) tracts usually have 3 neurons; descending (motor) tracts have 2 - an upper motor neuron and a lower motor neuron
  • Named origin → destination (spinothalamic = spinal cord → thalamus) · paired left and right · most cross the midline (decussate)
  • Sensory chain
    • 1st order: cell body in the dorsal root ganglion (pseudounipolar), brings the signal into the cord
    • 2nd order: cell body in the dorsal horn or a brainstem nucleus; its axon crosses and runs to the thalamus
    • 3rd order: ventral posterior lateral nucleus (VPL) of the thalamus → internal capsule → primary somatosensory cortex
  • Motor chain
    • upper motor neuron (UMN): cell body in the cortex or brainstem; axon crosses and synapses on a lower motor neuron
    • lower motor neuron (LMN): cell body in the ventral horn (body) or a cranial nerve motor nucleus (head) → muscle

blocks.alt: spinal cord cross-section ascending and descending tracts - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Spinal cord cross-section: ascending tracts (blue) and descending tracts (red), with the sacral-to-cervical layering inside each

blocks.html: 2. The tract table

cols: Sign of a one-sided cord lesion
rows: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus (gracilis = leg, cuneatus = arm)
Medulla - 2nd-order axons cross as the medial lemniscus
Lost on the same side below the lesion
Spinal cord, at the level of entry - anterior white commissure
Lost on the opposite side below the lesion
Posterior: never · anterior: crosses twice - both end on the same side
UMN weakness on the same side below the lesion
~10% stay uncrossed until their level, then act on both sides
Muscles of the head and face via cranial nerve nuclei
Mostly both sides - except the lower face (VII), opposite side only

blocks.html: 3. Dorsal column-medial lemniscus

• 1st order: up the same side in the fasciculus gracilis (leg) or fasciculus cuneatus (arm)
  • 2nd order: nucleus gracilis / nucleus cuneatus in the medulla → axons cross → medial lemniscus → VPL
  • 3rd order: VPL → internal capsule → primary somatosensory cortex
  • (sources differ: one section of the note says the nucleus gracilis takes sensation from above T6 (arms) and the cuneatus from below; the note's own pathway section and the upper-year notes say gracilis = leg (below T6), cuneatus = arm - check the slides)

blocks.alt: medulla oblongata cross-section (nucleus gracilis, nucleus cuneatus, and medial lamniscus).png
blocks.cap: The medulla: nucleus gracilis and cuneatus send fibres across the midline to form the medial lemniscus

blocks.html: 4. Spinothalamic tract

• 1st order: synapses straight away in the dorsal horn
  • 2nd order: crosses at once in the anterior white commissure → up the opposite side → VPL
  • 3rd order: VPL → internal capsule → primary somatosensory cortex
  • Pain and temperature fibres sit toward the edge of the cord
5. Spinocerebellar tracts

• Simplest pathway: no thalamus and no net crossing - unconscious position sense for staying upright
  • 1st order from muscle proprioceptors (spindles, Golgi tendon organs) → dorsal horn
  • Posterior tract: same side → inferior cerebellar peduncle (medulla) · anterior tract: crosses, then crosses back → superior cerebellar peduncle
6. Descending motor tracts

• Lateral corticospinal: primary motor cortex → corona radiata → internal capsule → cerebral peduncle (midbrain) → ventral pons → medullary pyramids → ~90% cross → lateral white column → synapse on LMNs in the ventral horn → limbs
  • Corticobulbar: motor cortex → internal capsule → cerebral peduncle → branches to the pons and medulla → LMNs in the nuclei of III, IV, V, VII, IX, X, XI, XII
    • the lower face gets only crossed input, the forehead both → a UMN facial nerve palsy spares the forehead

blocks.cap: Corticobulbar pathway: motor cortex to the cranial nerve nuclei in the pons and medulla

blocks.html: 7. Cerebellar connections

• In: spinocerebellar tracts (inferior and superior peduncles) · corticopontocerebellar: motor cortex → pontine nuclei → cross → middle cerebellar peduncle → cerebellar hemisphere
  • Out: deep cerebellar nuclei → superior peduncle → opposite thalamus (ventral lateral nucleus) → motor cortex
  • Input and output both cross, so the cerebellum acts on the same side of the body

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of Sensation
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of sensation
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Vibration, fine touch and position cross in the medulla; pain and temperature cross in the cord where they enter - so a cord hemisection loses position sense on the lesion's side and pain on the other. Pacinian = vibration, Meissner = texture, Merkel = edges, Ruffini = stretch. Test pain or temperature, not touch, to find a segmental level. Burning and freezing are felt by pain receptors. Gracilis = leg, cuneatus = arm.

blocks.html: Each skin receptor reports one kind of touch, and two pathways carry it to the cortex - one crossing in the medulla, one in the cord. That split is what lets a cord lesion separate vibration from pain.
1. Receptors in the skin

• Free nerve endings: around hair follicles (very sensitive), pain and temperature
  • Nociceptors (pain)
    • on a myelinated axon: fast, sharp, well localized → can trigger withdrawal
    • on an unmyelinated axon: slow, dull, throbbing, poorly localized
  • Thermoreceptors: one for warm, one for cool · burning or freezing activates pain receptors, not thermoreceptors

blocks.cap: Skin receptors by depth: Merkel disc and Meissner corpuscle near the surface, Pacinian corpuscle and Ruffini ending deep in the dermis

blocks.html: 2. How a stimulus is coded

• Pacinian corpuscle: pressure deforms the capsule → stretch-gated ion channels open → receptor potential → action potential if threshold is reached
  • Stronger, longer stimulus → faster, longer train of action potentials, but the curve flattens at high pressure → easier to tell 4 g from 5 g than 14 g from 15 g
  • Labelled lines: each receptor has its own "private line", so what you feel depends on which axon fires - hitting the ulnar nerve at the elbow (funny bone) is felt in the fingers
  • Acuity: few afferents converge per neuron at the fingertip (small fields, fine two-point discrimination) vs many on the back · centre-surround inhibition sharpens edges
  • Touch is needed for fine motor control: numb the fingertips and lighting a match becomes hard
3. The two pathways

rows: Up the same side in the dorsal column → nucleus gracilis (leg) or nucleus cuneatus (arm) in the medulla
Synapses in the dorsal horn at the level it enters

blocks.html: • Dorsal columns are layered: at the neck, leg fibres lie medially, then trunk, then arm laterally (new fibres join on the outside)

blocks.alt: dorsal column-medial lemniscus vs spinothalamic pathway - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway (crossing in the medulla) beside the spinothalamic tract (crossing in the spinal cord)

blocks.html: 4. Clinical use

• Cord hemisection: the tracts run in different columns and cross at different levels, so a right hemisection loses
    • vibration, fine touch and proprioception on the right (same side)
    • pain and temperature on the left (opposite side)
  • Dermatomes (skin supplied by one spinal nerve) overlap - more for touch than for pain and temperature
    • so test pain or temperature to find the level of a segmental nerve injury
5. Somatosensory cortex

• Primary somatosensory cortex = postcentral gyrus · four strips, each with its own body map (homunculus): proprioception · touch · texture · size and shape
  • The map is plastic: a heavily used part grows (a violinist's fingering hand); after an amputation neighbouring areas take over - stroking the face can be felt in the missing hand

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of the Cerebellum and Basal Ganglia
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of the cerebellum and basal ganglia
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Cerebellar disease = intention tremor, low tone, signs on the same side, stable or improving; Parkinson disease = tremor at rest, rigidity, trouble starting, progressive - and neither causes weakness. Dopamine turns GO up and NO-GO down: too little → Parkinson, too much levodopa → dyskinesia. Huntington chorea = lost striatum, too little NO-GO. Cerebellar lesions last because the repair shop itself is broken.

blocks.html: Two side loops tune movement without commanding it: the cerebellum corrects errors and learns skills, the basal ganglia choose which movement is released. Damage gives movement disorders without weakness - and the tremor, tone and course tell them apart.
1. Side loops in the motor system

• Both take input from wide areas of the cortex and send output through the thalamus back to the cortex (and to the brainstem)
  • Neither sends its own tract to the spinal cord, so they have no upper motor neurons → not upper motor neuron (UMN) disorders
2. Cerebellum: what it does

• Folded into folia and fissures · holds half of all the brain's neurons
  • Corrects errors in movement commands and learns motor skills
    • in: motor and somatosensory cortex, brainstem, spinal cord · out: motor cortex, brainstem and cord
  • Lesions show on the same side: each half works with the opposite motor cortex, which moves the opposite body - so a right cerebellar lesion affects the right limbs
  • How it learns (upper-year notes)
    • mossy fibres → parallel fibres → Purkinje cell = "what I did" (the student)
    • climbing fibres from the inferior olive = "something is wrong" (the teacher, an error signal) → reshape the parallel-fibre synapses
    • e.g. re-tuning the vestibulo-ocular reflex with new glasses · cerebellar patients cannot adapt their aim when prism goggles shift what they see
  • "Repair shop": it masks motor damage elsewhere, so cerebellar lesions themselves cause longer-lasting problems
3. Cerebellar signs

rows: Wide-based, drunk-looking gait · nystagmus (broken vestibulo-ocular reflex)
Gait ataxia - falls walking heel-to-toe · hypotonia
Dysmetria (misses the target) · dyssynergia (body segments poorly coordinated) · intention tremor (worst at the end of a movement) · fails finger-to-nose

blocks.html: • Romberg (feet together, eyes open then closed): sways with eyes open and closed = cerebellar · sways only with eyes closed = sensory ataxia (sources differ: the upper-year notes also list a Romberg sign under vestibulocerebellar damage - check the slides)

blocks.alt: cerebellum functional zones vermis intermediate lateral - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Cerebellum from behind: vermis, intermediate and lateral zones; anterior, posterior and flocculonodular lobes
Finger-to-nose: a normal straight path against the wandering path of cerebellar dysmetria

blocks.html: 4. Basal ganglia: release and suppress

• Release the wanted movement, suppress the inappropriate ones from the premotor and motor cortex · damage contributes to Tourette syndrome (inappropriate utterances released)
  • In: cortex → striatum (caudate + putamen) · out: globus pallidus → thalamus → cortex
  • Modulators: subthalamic nucleus → globus pallidus · substantia nigra → striatum
  • Dopamine from the substantia nigra excites the direct pathway (GO) and damps the indirect pathway (NO-GO)
  • Eye movements: the substantia nigra holds the superior colliculus in check; the striatum lifts that brake to release a saccade
5. Basal ganglia disorders

• Levodopa = dopamine precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier - the main treatment for Parkinson disease
  • (sources differ on Huntington: the note says ↑ dopamine causes the under-inhibition; the anatomy lecture note and the upper-year notes blame loss of the striatum's indirect pathway - check the slides)
6. Cerebellar disease vs Parkinson disease

rows: Ataxia: starts, but inaccurate (dysmetria) and poorly coordinated (dyssynergia)
Akinesia: can't start (may need an outside cue) · bradykinesia: slow
Intention - end of a movement, none at rest

lectures.name: Neurophysiology of Reflexes
lectures.title: Neurophysiology of reflexes
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Upper motor neuron lesion = spastic, brisk reflexes, clonus, upgoing big toe, no wasting (flaccid only in the first days); lower motor neuron lesion = flaccid, absent reflexes, fasciculations, wasting. Spindle = length, Ia, monosynaptic stretch reflex; Golgi tendon organ = force, Ib, relaxes the muscle. Small, fatigue-resistant units are recruited first. Fasciculation = whole motor unit (visible); fibrillation = one fibre (EMG only). Supplementary motor area lesion → apraxia.

blocks.html: From the motor unit up to the motor cortex: how force is graded, how muscle sensors drive the spinal reflexes, and why a lesion above or below the lower motor neuron looks so different at the bedside.
1. Lower motor neurons and motor units

• Lower motor neuron (LMN) = synapses directly on muscle · cell body in the ventral horn (body) or a cranial nerve nucleus (head and neck)
    • alpha motor neurons → force · gamma motor neurons → keep the muscle spindle taut
  • Motor unit = one alpha motor neuron + all the muscle fibres it supplies (the smallest unit of control) · motor neuron pool = all the alpha motor neurons to one muscle
  • Innervation ratio (fibres per neuron)
    • small (<10, eye and finger muscles) → fine, precise control
    • large (>1000, e.g. the quadriceps) → big, less precise force
  • Fibre types: red (oxidative, fatigue-resistant, slow, small neurons) · white (glycolytic, fatigable, fast and powerful, large neurons)
2. Grading muscle force
Action potentials are all-or-none, so force is graded two ways:

• Rate coding: fire faster → twitches sum and fuse (tetanus)
  • Size principle: small, fatigue-resistant units are recruited first; large units join only for big, brief efforts

blocks.cap: Size principle: slow fatigue-resistant units carry standing and walking; fast fatigable units are added for running and jumping

blocks.html: 3. Neuromuscular junction and spontaneous firing

• Neuromuscular junction: one of the body's largest synapses · one action potential releases enough acetylcholine to contract the unit
    • target of toxins (botulinum toxin, curare) and disease (myasthenia gravis)

rows: Irritable motor neuron or axon injury before the muscle → LMN problem
A whole muscle or group (the pool)

blocks.html: 4. Muscle sensors

rows: Would fall silent - gamma motor neurons keep it taut (alpha-gamma co-activation)

blocks.html: • Keeping the spindle "online" during contraction lets it catch an unexpected stretch mid-movement
5. Spinal reflexes

rows: Ia axon synapses directly on the alpha motor neuron of the same muscle and its synergists · an inhibitory interneuron relaxes the antagonist
Muscle contracts back against the stretch - the basis of deep tendon reflexes
Ib axon → inhibitory interneuron to the same muscle
Muscle eases off → steady tension (holding a paper cup without crushing it)
Many synapses, both sides of the cord
Stepped-on leg flexes away, the other leg extends to keep balance

blocks.html:
• Descending pathways normally hold the stretch reflex down → it becomes exaggerated after spinal cord injury
  • Central pattern generators: the cord alone can produce the walking rhythm → used in locomotor therapy after spinal cord injury

blocks.cap: Monosynaptic stretch reflex: a passive stretch excites the spindle, Ia afferents fire the same muscle and inhibit its antagonist

blocks.alt: flexion and crossed extension reflex - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Flexion-crossed extension: the stimulated leg flexes while the opposite leg extends

blocks.html: 6. Motor cortex and the corticospinal tracts

• Primary motor cortex has a motor homunculus: face and hand get the most cortex (finest control) · it maps movements, not single muscles
  • Lateral corticospinal tract: longest tract in the central nervous system (so easily damaged), ~1 million axons, not mature at birth
    • from ⅓ primary motor, ⅓ premotor and supplementary motor, ⅓ primary somatosensory cortex
    • crosses at the pyramidal decussation → lateral column → synapses on LMNs → distal limb, fine finger movement
  • Anterior corticospinal tract: smaller, no sensory-cortex input · stays uncrossed to its level, then acts on both sides → trunk and posture
7. Upper vs lower motor neuron lesions

rows: Spastic - but flaccid for the first days, spastic after about a week

blocks.html: • A small motor cortex lesion may only cost independent finger movement on the opposite side
8. The motor hierarchy

• Prefrontal and posterior parietal cortex → premotor and supplementary motor area → primary motor cortex · higher = more abstract
  • Supplementary motor area lesion → apraxia (complex motor acts lost, simple movements intact) · one-sided lesion, two-sided deficit
  • Prefrontal cortex = rules and context → lesions fail the Wisconsin card-sorting task
  • Posterior parietal cortex = spatial attention → hemispatial neglect after parietal stroke

lectures.name: Spinal Cord
lectures.title: Spinal cord
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anterior cord spares vibration and position; posterior cord spares movement; central cord hits the arms harder than the legs; Brown-Séquard loses power and position on the lesion's side and pain and temperature on the other. Complete injury = no rectal tone and no perianal sensation. Test pain to find the level. Cervical cord lesion = UMN signs in arms and legs; cervical root = LMN signs in one arm. Bilateral leg symptoms with bladder or bowel loss and saddle numbness → cauda equina.

blocks.html: Find the level, then the pattern: a sensory level and the upper-vs-lower motor neuron signs say where the lesion is; which modalities are lost, and on which side, say which part of the cord it hits.
1. Three pathways that decide the pattern

cols: One-sided cord lesion loses it on

blocks.html: 2. Assessing the cord

• Sensory
    • light touch travels in both sensory tracts · pain (spinothalamic only) maps dermatomes most precisely
    • look for a sensory level
  • Motor: bulk, tone, power, reflexes · myotomes (muscles supplied by one spinal nerve, tested as joint movements, e.g. elbow flexion) · decide upper motor neuron (UMN) vs lower motor neuron (LMN)
  • The American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Scale tests every major root
3. Cord (myelopathy) vs root (radiculopathy)

rows: Both legs ± bowel and bladder - the usual thoracic picture
One leg - but think of cauda equina syndrome

blocks.html: • Radiculopathy: radiating pain, numbness in a dermatome, LMN weakness in a myotome · discectomy takes pressure off the root
4. Complete vs incomplete injury

• Complete: no motor or sensory function below the level, including lost rectal tone and perianal sensation
  • Incomplete: some function below the level · the pattern depends on which part of the cord is hit (section 5)
5. Incomplete cord syndromes

rows: Anterior spinal artery blocked (atherosclerosis, aortic disease) · compression (disc, tumour) · trauma
Autonomic: orthostatic low blood pressure, bladder, bowel, sexual
Posterior spinal artery blocked · compression · vitamin B12 deficiency, syphilis
Hyperextension injury - commonest pattern in elderly trauma · syrinx (cyst), tumour, demyelination
Arm fibres lie innermost in the lateral corticospinal tract
Trauma, disease inside the cord · rare, usually incomplete

blocks.html: • Cauda equina syndrome (below the cord, nerve roots): both legs - pain, saddle anesthesia, loss of bowel and bladder control · LMN-pattern paraparesis

blocks.cap: The four incomplete cord syndromes: which part of the cord is damaged and where motor and sensory function is lost
Lateral corticospinal tract layering: arm fibres innermost, then trunk, then leg - why central cord injury hits the arms first

lectures.name: Neurophthalmology
lectures.title: Neuro-ophthalmology
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anisocoria worse in the light = parasympathetic (pupil cannot constrict); worse in the dark = sympathetic (pupil cannot dilate). A third nerve palsy with a blown pupil is compressive (aneurysm); pupil-sparing is microvascular (diabetes). Fourth = head tilt; sixth = head turn toward the weak side, and think raised intracranial pressure. RAPD = optic nerve on that side. Bitemporal hemianopia = chiasm = pituitary tumour. Jerk nystagmus is named by its fast phase.

blocks.html: Visual symptoms that do not come from the eyeball itself: double vision, eyes that will not hold still, unequal or sluggish pupils, and a missing part of the visual field. Each one points to a place along the nerves and brain pathways, so the lecture is really about localizing.
1. Double vision (diplopia)

• Diplopia = the two eyes are not aligned
    • one eye fixes the target on the fovea (the real image, in the centre) · the other eye's image lands off the fovea (the false image, off to the side)
    • concomitant (non-paralytic): the misalignment is the same in every direction of gaze · muscles work but are not pointed at the same place
    • incomitant (paralytic): the misalignment changes with the direction of gaze · a nerve or muscle is not working (palsy, fracture)
    • other causes besides a nerve palsy: thyroid eye disease · myasthenia gravis
  • Causes of a nerve palsy: ischemia (diabetes, high blood pressure) · aneurysm · tumour · trauma
    • investigations: CT of the head and neck · angiogram · blood work for inflammation (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) to look for giant cell arteritis

rows: Medial, superior and inferior rectus · inferior oblique · levator palpebrae (lid) · pupil constrictor
Down and out · ptosis · may have a large pupil
Compressive (aneurysm) → "blown" pupil, because the pupil fibres run on the outside of the nerve · microvascular (diabetes) → pupil spared
Up and in · trouble looking down and in · vertical double vision
Head tilt · often congenital or after trauma (longest, thinnest nerve) · the least worrying
Turned in · cannot abduct · horizontal double vision
Head turn toward the affected side · can be a sign of raised intracranial pressure (long course from pons to skull base) → with a headache, think raised pressure

blocks.html: 2. Nystagmus

• Nystagmus = an eye movement disorder: the eyes drift slowly off the target, then come back
    • pendular: both phases slow, the eyes "wobble"
    • jerk: slow drift away, fast snap back · named by the direction of the fast phase ("beats" that way) · the most common type
  • Gaze-evoked nystagmus = cannot hold the eyes off-centre
    • beats in the direction of gaze (left-beating on left gaze, up-beating on upgaze, and so on)
    • the gaze-holding circuit lives in the brainstem and cerebellum, so a lesion lets the eyes drift back to the middle, then they saccade out again - an "ataxia of the eyes"
    • Causes
      • structural (cerebellum or brainstem): stroke · bleed · tumour · demyelination · degeneration (alcohol)
      • inherited: hereditary ataxias
      • toxins: alcohol · phenytoin (Dilantin) and other antiseizure drugs · lithium
3. The pupil
• Pupil size is a tug of war: parasympathetic constricts, sympathetic dilates

rows: Optic nerve (the afferent) → pretectal nucleus (midbrain) → both Edinger-Westphal nuclei → cranial nerve III → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves

1st neuron: hypothalamus → down to C8-T1 (ciliospinal centre) · 2nd: over the lung apex, under the subclavian artery, up to the superior cervical ganglion · 3rd: along the internal carotid, through the cavernous sinus → long ciliary nerves
Bilateral pretectal output = why both pupils constrict to light in one eye (consensual response)
Also lifts the lid a couple of millimetres (Müller's muscle) - wide eyes when scared

blocks.alt: pupillary light reflex pathway - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Pupillary light reflex: optic nerve to the pretectal area, then both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, cranial nerve III and the ciliary ganglion to each constrictor

blocks.html: • Anisocoria (unequal pupils): ask is it worse in the light or the dark?

or in the dark?"} B -->|"Worse in LIGHT"| C["The big pupil fails to CONSTRICT
PARASYMPATHETIC problem
e.g. compressive third nerve palsy"] B -->|"Worse in DARK"| D["The small pupil fails to DILATE
SYMPATHETIC problem
e.g. Horner syndrome"]

blocks.html: • Horner syndrome = sympathetic damage: small pupil (miosis) · mild ptosis · no sweating (anhidrosis) on that side · Kai's example was an arterial dissection (full detail in 14 - Autonomic Nervous System)
4. Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)

• RAPD = a very sensitive sign of a one-sided optic nerve problem (the afferent arm of the light reflex)
  • Found with the swinging flashlight test
    • light in the good eye → both pupils constrict fully
    • swing to the bad eye → less light is "seen", so both pupils dilate (paradoxically)
  • The other pupil's pathway is intact, which is why it is relative
5. Visual field defects

• Nasal retinal fibres cross at the chiasm; temporal fibres do not → each side of the brain sees the opposite visual field
  • Pathway: optic nerve → chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus (thalamus) → optic radiations → occipital cortex

rows: Bitemporal hemianopia - the commonest cause is a pituitary tumour

lectures.name: Cortical Syndromes
lectures.title: Cortical syndromes
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Aphasia = dominant hemisphere; neglect = non-dominant hemisphere. Broca's (frontal) = halting speech, understanding intact; Wernicke's (temporal) = fluent nonsense, understanding lost - and attention is normal, unlike delirium. Any cortical sign rules out a pure subcortical or brainstem lesion. Cortical sensory signs only count if primary sensation is intact. Test comprehension with motor, not verbal, commands.

blocks.html: Some deficits can only come from the cortex, so finding one tells you where the lesion is. Language problems point to the dominant hemisphere; neglect points to the non-dominant one.
1. Why cortical signs matter: cortex, subcortex or brainstem
• Cortical syndromes help localize (for example, a stroke), explain the presentation, and show that something is wrong

rows: Aphasia · neglect · apraxia · cortical sensory signs (agraphesthesia, astereognosis) · isolated homonymous hemianopia
Pure motor weakness of one side · pure sensory change of one side (face, arm, leg) · ataxic hemiparesis (mild clumsiness + mild weakness)
vertigo plus another symptom · diplopia plus another symptom · crossed sensory loss (face one side, body the other)

blocks.html: 2. The dominant hemisphere

• Dominant = the hemisphere that handles language
    • right-handed people: almost always the left
    • left-handed people: left in 60% · right in about 20% · both in about 20%
  • A middle cerebral artery stroke on the dominant side usually disturbs language
3. Aphasia

• Aphasia = a disorder of language (making or understanding it), from the dominant hemisphere
    • not the same as dysarthria, which is a problem articulating speech

rows: Slow, halting, effortful · none at all if severe · paraphasic errors (wrong sounds or words)
Fluent but meaningless · real words that do not hang together, or no recognizable language if severe

blocks.html:
• ⚠ Wernicke's aphasia is often mistaken for delirium - but attention is normal in aphasia
  • How to test language (start easy, get harder):

rows: Cannot name a watch or pen
Names the object, not its parts (watch face, pen cap)
Motor commands, not verbal ones (close your eyes, stick out your tongue, point to the ceiling)
Open question or describe a picture · nonsense said fluently still counts as fluent
Repeat a phrase ("no ifs, ands, or buts", or the MoCA sentences)

blocks.html: 4. Apraxia

• Apraxia = cannot carry out a motor task despite having the strength to do it
  • Usually the dominant parietal or frontal lobe
  • Examples: cannot pretend to use a hammer, whistle, make a hand posture, draw, get dressed
    • subtypes (ideomotor, ideational, constructional, orofacial) - the medwiki note says you do not need them all for the exam
5. Neglect

• Neglect = does not attend to one side, though sensation is intact · usually the non-dominant hemisphere
    • visual: ignores one side of space, yet still blinks to a threat there (so it is attention, not sight)
    • sensory: ignores touch on one side
    • asomatognosia: does not recognize their own limb (thinks the arm is the examiner's)
    • anosognosia: unaware of having a deficit at all
6. Cortical sensory signs and extinction

• Primary sensation must be intact for these to localize to the cortex · a loss of pinprick, temperature, pressure, vibration or light touch can come from anywhere along the sensory tract
    • Agraphesthesia: cannot read a number traced on the skin
    • Astereognosis: cannot identify an object by touch alone (but can once they see it)
    • position sense: cannot tell which way a stimulus on the skin is moving
  • Extinction: feels a stimulus on either side alone, but when both sides are touched at once, misses the affected side
    • sensory extinction → parietal lobe · visual extinction → occipital lobe

lectures.name: Approach to Weakness
lectures.title: Approach to weakness
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ No sensory loss narrows LMN weakness to three places: anterior horn cell (segmental), neuromuscular junction (fatigable, eyes first) or muscle (proximal, symmetric). UMN = spastic, brisk, upgoing toe, pyramidal (arm extensors and leg flexors weak); LMN = floppy, reduced reflexes, wasting, fasciculations. A sensory level means spinal cord. Polyneuropathy is distal; myopathy is proximal.

blocks.html: Weakness can come from anywhere between the cerebrum and the muscle fibre. First decide upper motor neuron (UMN) or lower motor neuron (LMN); then let the pattern and the company it keeps (sensory loss, pain, cranial nerves, bladder) pin down the level.
1. The approach

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["True weakness?
rule out mimics: incoordination · apraxia · severe sensory loss"] --> B{"Upper or lower
motor neuron signs?"} B -->|"UMN: spastic, brisk reflexes,
upgoing toe, pyramidal pattern"| C{"Which level?"} C -->|"Hemiparesis + cortical signs
(aphasia, neglect, seizures)"| D["BRAIN"] C -->|"Hemiparesis + cranial nerve signs,
cerebellar signs, crossed sensory loss"| E["BRAINSTEM"] C -->|"Paraparesis or quadriparesis
+ sensory level, bladder, back or neck pain"| F["SPINAL CORD"] B -->|"LMN: floppy, reduced reflexes,
wasting, fasciculations"| G{"Sensory loss?"} G -->|"None"| H{"Pattern?"} H -->|"Segmental"| I["ANTERIOR HORN CELL"] H -->|"Fluctuating, fatigable,
eyes first"| J["NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION"] H -->|"Symmetric, proximal"| K["MUSCLE"] G -->|"Yes"| L{"Pattern?"} L -->|"One myotome + dermatome,
radiating pain"| M["NERVE ROOT"] L -->|"Many roots, painful,
saddle anesthesia"| N["MULTIPLE ROOTS
(cauda equina)"] L -->|"One limb, more than
one nerve or root"| O["PLEXUS"] L -->|"One nerve's muscles"| P["MONONEUROPATHY"] L -->|"Distal, symmetric,
glove and stocking"| Q["POLYNEUROPATHY"]

blocks.html:
• History: which areas (one limb, one side, both sides) · onset (sudden or gradual) · what tasks are hard · other symptoms (sensory change, speech or swallowing, pain, bowel or bladder for cord or low roots)
  • Exam: confirms the site, extent and character · look for mild weakness and side-to-side differences
  • Medical Research Council (MRC) power scale
2. Upper vs lower motor neuron

rows: Corticospinal pathway: cortex · white matter · internal capsule · brainstem · spinal cord
Anterior horn cell → root → plexus → nerve → neuromuscular junction → muscle
Depends on the cause · smaller area
↑ (loss of the brake on spinal reflexes)
Yes (a motor unit firing on its own · can be normal, e.g. an eyelid twitch)

blocks.html:
• Pyramidal weakness (UMN):
    • arms: extensors weaker than flexors (triceps < biceps, wrist extension < flexion)
    • legs: flexors weaker than extensors (knee flexion < extension, dorsiflexion < plantar flexion)
    • one explanation: upright humans keep strong arm flexors (feeding) and leg extensors (walking)

blocks.alt: distribution of weakness by lesion site - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Where the weakness falls for a hemispheric, brainstem, spinal cord, root, nerve, polyneuropathy and muscle lesion

blocks.html: 3. Upper motor neuron localizations

rows: Hemiparesis, pyramidal · face + arm > leg = middle cerebral artery · leg > face + arm = anterior cerebral artery · face = arm = leg = internal capsule
Cranial nerve signs (double vision, vertigo, facial weakness) · cerebellar signs · crossed sensory loss (face one side, body the other)
Sensory level (normal above a line, impaired below; umbilicus = T10) · neck or back pain · bladder symptoms
Trauma · disc herniation · tumour · epidural hematoma · multiple sclerosis

blocks.html: 4. Lower motor neuron localizations

rows: Polio and polio-like illness · ALS (but also has UMN signs)
Dermatomal · pain from neck or back into a limb
Many muscles over more than one level, sometimes both sides
One limb, more muscles than one nerve or root
Ulnar, radial, common peroneal, sciatic palsies
Fluctuating, fatigable · eyes first (ptosis, double vision), then speech and swallowing
Symmetric, proximal (neck, trunk, shoulder and hip girdle)
Inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis, dermatomyositis) · muscular dystrophies

blocks.html:
• Kai's worked cases, in one line each
    • trouble with stairs and dressing, proximal weakness, normal reflexes and sensation → muscle
    • numb feet, weak ankles, absent ankle reflexes, distal sensory loss → peripheral nerve
    • weak legs, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, upgoing toes, sensory loss up to the trunk → spinal cord

lectures.name: Approach to Localization
lectures.title: Approach to localization
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Any cortical sign puts the lesion in the cortex; vertigo or double vision plus something else, or crossed face-body sensory loss, puts it in the brainstem; pure motor or pure sensory without either puts it in the subcortex. MCA = face and arm > leg; ACA = leg > face and arm; PCA = hemianopia with macular sparing. Sudden = vascular; subacute = inflammation, infection or tumour. Cerebellar lesion = same-side signs. Dysarthria spares language; aphasia does not.

blocks.html: Before naming a disease, say where the lesion is. Describe the problem (tempo and deficits), localize it with neuroanatomy, and only then build a differential - the time course tells you what kind of lesion, the signs tell you where.
1. The approach

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["1. DESCRIBE the problem
onset: acute · subacute · chronic
course: progressive · intermittent · stable
deficits: cognitive · motor · sensory · coordination"] --> B["2. LOCALIZE the lesion"] B --> C{"Any cortical sign?
aphasia · neglect · apraxia ·
cortical sensory loss · isolated hemianopia"} C -->|Yes| D["CORTEX"] C -->|No| E{"Cranial nerve signs, vertigo or
double vision + something else,
or crossed face / body sensory loss?"} E -->|Yes| F["BRAINSTEM"] E -->|No| G{"Pure motor, pure sensory
or ataxic hemiparesis?"} G -->|Yes| H["SUBCORTEX
(white matter tracts)"] D --> I["3. DIFFERENTIAL from the tempo
then investigations and management"] F --> I H --> I

blocks.html:
• Why subcortex for pure motor weakness: the motor strip is huge, so face, arm and leg are rarely all hit in the cortex · their fibres bundle together in the white matter, so a small deep lesion takes all three
  • Lesion type by time course
2. Stroke syndromes by artery

rows: Contralateral weakness and sensory loss, face + arm > leg · eyes look toward the lesion · homonymous hemianopia · aphasia (dominant side) or neglect (non-dominant side)
Contralateral weakness and sensory loss, leg > face + arm · apathy · apraxia · emotional change
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing · sensory symptoms if the lateral thalamus is involved
Ipsilateral facial paralysis · ↓ pain and temperature on the same-side face and opposite body · ↓ tears, saliva and taste (front of tongue) · vertigo, nystagmus · ataxia, dysmetria
Trouble swallowing or hoarseness · ↓ pain and temperature on the same-side face and opposite body · ipsilateral Horner syndrome · vertigo, nystagmus · ataxia
Contralateral paralysis · tongue deviates toward the lesion · loss of position sense

blocks.html: • Small penetrating arteries → lacunar syndromes (deep white matter, internal capsule, brainstem): clumsy hand-dysarthria · pure motor (face = arm = leg) · pure sensory · ataxic hemiparesis · sensorimotor

blocks.cap: Stroke syndromes for each artery: motor, sensory and pain-temperature loss drawn on the body

blocks.html: 3. Cerebellar lesions

• A lesion of the cerebellum gives ipsilateral signs · a lesion of its outflow beyond the cerebellar peduncles gives contralateral signs
  • Think of someone drunk (alcohol is a cerebellar toxin):
    • nystagmus · ataxic (scanning) dysarthria · trouble swallowing
    • finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin ataxia · dysdiadochokinesia (clumsy rapid alternating movements)
    • wide, unsteady gait · cannot walk heel-to-toe (tandem)
  • Cerebellar signs can come from anywhere on the pathway: subcortical white matter, thalamus, midbrain, pons, cerebellum
4. Dysarthria vs aphasia
• Dysarthria = trouble articulating: naming, comprehension, repetition and fluency are all normal · aphasia affects these

rows: Flaccid: nasal, because a weak palate cannot close off the nose
Cortex (mouth area of the motor strip) · subcortex · thalamus · brainstem · cerebellum and its pathways (ataxic dysarthria)
Nerve (e.g. recurrent laryngeal) · neuromuscular junction (myasthenia gravis) · muscle

lectures.name: Neuroembryology
lectures.title: Neuroembryology
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Front neuropore fails = anencephaly; back neuropore fails = spina bifida - and folic acid helps prevent both. Myelomeningocele has cord outside; meningocele has only meninges; occulta is a dimple or hair tuft. Neuronal migration disorders present with drug-resistant epilepsy. Neural tube = central nervous system; neural crest = peripheral and enteric nervous system. Diencephalon makes the retina and the third ventricle.

blocks.html: The whole nervous system comes from ectoderm: the neural tube becomes the central nervous system and the neural crest the peripheral one. Most of the pathology in this lecture is a step that failed: a neuropore that did not close, or neurons that did not migrate.
1. Ectoderm and its three fates

rows: Peripheral and enteric (gut) nervous system · glia · pigment cells (melanocytes) · cartilage and bone of the face and skull · smooth muscle
Epidermis · hair · nails · sebaceous glands · olfactory and mouth lining · eyes

blocks.html:
• The neural plate appears at about day 18, folds, and closes into the tube
    • cranial (front) neuropore closes by day 24-25 · caudal (back) neuropore by day 26-28
  • Cells: neuroepithelial cells are the stem cells (they make radial glia, which give rise to neurons and glia) · a neuroblast has stopped dividing and will become a neuron after it migrates
2. Brain vesicles

blocks.cap: The three primary vesicles: prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), rhombencephalon (hindbrain)

rows: Cerebrum: cortex, white matter, basal ganglia

blocks.html: 3. Timeline of brain development

• In order:
    • neurogenesis: neurons multiply from the lining of the tube, first symmetrically, then explosively
    • gliogenesis: follows, peaks around birth, continues after
    • migration: neurons travel out along glial fibres to the cortical plate · genetically controlled, so genetic syndromes can disrupt it
    • synaptogenesis: needs astrocytes · starts in the cortex at about weeks 24-27 and continues into early adulthood
    • myelination: last, mostly after birth · runs from the front of the brain backward · myelin damps down new synapses and plasticity
  • Kai: synapse density peaks at about age 6, then pruning thins them out

blocks.cap: Brain development from neural tube to adulthood: neurulation, migration and neurogenesis early; synaptogenesis, gliogenesis and myelination late

blocks.html: 4. Spinal cord development

• The caudal two-thirds of the tube becomes the spinal cord; its cavity becomes the central canal
  • The wall splits into a mantle layer (deep, future grey matter) and a marginal layer (surface, future white matter)
  • Alar and basal plates
    • alar plate → dorsal horn (sensory) · basal plate → ventral horn (motor) · intermediate plate → lateral horn (sympathetic)
    • (sources differ: the medwiki note's text has these the other way round, but its own figure labels the alar plate dorsal and sensory and the basal plate ventral and motor - check the slides)
  • The spine outgrows the cord: at birth the cord fills the canal · the spine keeps growing and the cord does not, so it ends at about L1 and the nerve roots carry on as the cauda equina

blocks.cap: Developing spinal cord: alar plate becomes the sensory dorsal horn, basal plate the motor ventral horn

blocks.html: 5. Neural tube defects

rows: Born without parts of the brain and skull (forebrain usually missing) · about 1 in 4,500
No treatment; almost all die soon after birth
Caudal neuropore or anywhere along the lower tube
Usually lumbar · disability depends on size, level and whether nerves are involved

blocks.html:
• Spina bifida, worst to mildest:
    • Myelomeningocele: meninges, nerves and spinal cord outside the body · highest risk of cord damage
    • Meningocele: meninges only, cord and nerves stay in
    • Spina bifida occulta: a sacral dimple, sometimes a tuft of hair · no real symptoms, often found by chance
  • Prevention: folic acid in pregnancy, for both (sources: both the medwiki note and Kai write "400 mg" - check the units on the slides)
  • Screening: alpha-fetoprotein (amniocentesis) · ultrasound
  • Causes: genetic, chromosomal and environmental (including medicines)
6. Neuronal migration disorders

• Neuronal migration disorders = neurons migrate abnormally in month 2, so the cortex is wrongly organized
    • the near-universal symptom is epilepsy that does not respond to drugs

rows: "Smooth brain": no normal gyri or sulci · small head
Many die before age 10 (aspiration, infections, seizures) · trouble swallowing, failure to thrive, seizures
Alone or with other malformations · late milestones, poor left-right coordination, social processing problems
Too many small folds · cortex simplified from 6 layers to 2-3
Often around the Sylvian fissure · linked to infection in pregnancy, low oxygen, chromosomal causes · delays and epilepsy

lectures.name: Autonomic Nervous System
lectures.title: Autonomic nervous system
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Horner = small pupil + mild ptosis + no sweating on the same side; a third nerve palsy = big pupil + severe ptosis + eye down and out. Sympathetic = thoracolumbar, short pre- and long postganglionic fibres; parasympathetic = cranial and sacral (S2-S4), long pre- and short postganglionic. A Pancoast tumour causes Horner by hitting the 2nd neuron over the lung apex. Parasympathetic empties the bladder; sympathetic holds it.

blocks.html: The autonomic nervous system runs smooth muscle, heart muscle and glands below the level of awareness, through two divisions that mostly pull in opposite directions. The clinical payoff is localizing a broken sympathetic chain to the eye (Horner syndrome) and recognizing autonomic failure in the bladder.
1. Organization
• The autonomic nervous system and the somatic nervous system are the two motor (efferent) arms of the peripheral nervous system

rows: Thoracolumbar cord (T1-L2; sources differ: Kai also writes T1-L3 - check the slides) · cell bodies in the lateral horn
Near the spine: sympathetic chain (paravertebral) and prevertebral ganglia around the celiac and mesenteric arteries
Divergent - one preganglionic neuron reaches many, so it fires all at once · the adrenal medulla acts as a postganglionic neuron, releasing epinephrine and norepinephrine into the blood

blocks.html: 2. What each division does

rows: Constricts skin and gut vessels · dilates vessels to skeletal muscle

blocks.alt: parasympathetic vs sympathetic organ effects - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Parasympathetic (left) and sympathetic (right) effects on each organ, with the cranial-sacral and thoracolumbar outflows

blocks.html: 3. Head and neck

• Sympathetic: preganglionic fibres leave at about T1-T2, enter the chain (white ramus), climb without synapsing, synapse in the superior cervical ganglion · postganglionic fibres ride the carotid arteries, then hitch a ride on trigeminal nerve branches to their targets
  • Parasympathetic: from brainstem nuclei via cranial nerves III, VII and IX to four ganglia · postganglionic fibres also travel on trigeminal branches

rows: Ciliary (orbit, between optic nerve and lateral rectus)
Via the carotid plexus and cavernous sinus → long ciliary nerves → pupil dilator and superior tarsal muscle (lifts the lid)

blocks.html: 4. Horner syndrome: where can the lesion be?

• Horner syndrome = the sympathetic supply to one side of the face is cut anywhere along its 3-neuron path · signs on the same side
    • miosis (small pupil - constriction is unopposed)
    • mild ptosis (the superior tarsal muscle loses its supply; the levator still works through cranial nerve III) (sources differ: one Kai passage blames the levator - check the slides)
    • anhidrosis (no sweating) · flushing from unopposed vasodilation

rows: Hypothalamus → down the brainstem and cord to C8-T1 (ciliospinal centre)
Leaves the cord → over the lung apex, under the subclavian artery → up the common carotid to the superior cervical ganglion
Along the internal carotid → cavernous sinus → with VI and V into the orbit → pupil dilator and Müller's (superior tarsal) muscle

blocks.html: • Causes named in the sources: neck trauma · Pancoast tumour (lung apex, where the 2nd neuron runs) · birth injury to the lower brachial plexus · an arterial dissection (the case in Kai's notes)

blocks.alt: oculosympathetic pathway three neurons - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The three-neuron sympathetic path to the eye: hypothalamus to C8-T1, over the lung apex to the superior cervical ganglion, then along the carotid to the pupil dilator and eyelid

blocks.html: 5. The bladder

rows: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (via the inferior hypogastric plexus)
Contracts the detrusor (empties) · relaxes the internal sphincter
Above the pelvic pain line → back with the sympathetics · below → with the parasympathetics

blocks.html: • Autonomic dysfunction of the bladder: urgency · incontinence · urinary tract infections from incomplete emptying

lectures.name: Neuroradiology
lectures.title: Neuroradiology
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Fluid is dark on T1, white on T2, and white on FLAIR except for CSF - so FLAIR makes edema stand out. On CT, acute blood is white and an acute infarct is dark. DWI = restricted diffusion = stroke; SWI = blood. Ultrasound and fluoroscopy have the best temporal resolution; MRI the best contrast; plain X-ray the best spatial.

blocks.html: Every imaging test trades three kinds of sharpness - detail, contrast and speed - against cost, availability and radiation. CT is fast and everywhere; MRI sees soft tissue best, and you choose its sequence for the question you are asking.
1. Three kinds of resolution

• Spatial: can you tell two nearby objects apart? (the amount of detail)
  • Contrast: can you tell apart two objects of similar density? (the range of greys)
  • Temporal: can you see change over time? (the time between images, as in a video)
2. The modalities

rows: X-rays blocked differently by tissues of different density (a shadow) · one view, one moment
Cheap · everywhere · instant · good for bone
A series of X-rays over time · one view, many moments · digital subtraction removes the baseline image so only new things (contrast dye) show
X-rays taken in a circle, combined into slices · many views, one (or a few) moments
Widely available · contrast dye improves contrast
Grayscale: time for sound to echo back · Doppler: frequency shift off moving blood (toward or away)
Protons in a changing magnetic and radiofrequency field · pick the sequences for the question

blocks.html: 3. CT of the brain

• Acute infarct = dark (low density) · acute hemorrhage = white · enlarged ventricles = hydrocephalus
  • Kai's CT signs of a stroke:
    • dense MCA sign: the clot in the middle cerebral artery seen directly, immediately
    • loss of grey-white differentiation (from edema) · insular ribbon sign (the insula is farthest from collateral flow) · lentiform sign (from about 1 hour)
    • sulcal effacement (swelling pushes the sulci closed) · later, a dark area matching one artery's territory
4. MRI sequences

rows: Edema · harder to see lesions right beside normal fluid
Edema stands out · also bleeding and other pathology
Restricted water movement (white) = high cellularity · stroke and hypercellular tumours · read with the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map
Blood: hemoglobin and hemosiderin show dark · exaggerates an artifact first seen on gradient echo

blocks.html:
• (sources differ on SWI: the medwiki note calls it excellent for strokes, Kai says it is only useful for blood - check the slides)
  • Usually 5 sequences at most, tailored to the clinical question

blocks.alt: MRI sequences T1 T2 FLAIR DWI SWI - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The same five sequences: T1 (CSF dark), T2 (CSF white), FLAIR (CSF dark, edema bright), DWI and SWI (dark spots of blood)

weeks.label: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections

lectures.name: Approach to Head Injuries
lectures.title: Approach to head injuries
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Epidural = arterial, lens-shaped, lucid interval; subdural = bridging veins, crescent, falls and the elderly. Uncal herniation blows the pupil on the same side. The Cushing triad is a late sign of raised pressure. Decerebrate (extensor) posturing is worse than decorticate (flexor). Diffuse axonal injury: deep coma with a near-normal CT. Concussion is clinical - most never lose consciousness, and a normal scan does not exclude it.

blocks.html: Every head injury is a trauma patient first: resuscitate, protect the neck, then grade the brain injury with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). The grade sets the path - a severe injury is a fight against raised intracranial pressure and herniation; a mild one (concussion) is a clinical diagnosis managed with brief rest and a graded return.
1. The approach to an acute head injury

flowchart TD A["Head injury"] --> B["Primary survey (Advanced Trauma Life Support)
Airway: intubate or hold the head in line · Breathing
Circulation: IV, bloods for drugs and clotting

collar + backboard"] C --> D{"GCS after resuscitation?"} D -->|"8 or less"| E["SEVERE
protect the airway · keep oxygen and perfusion up
CT head + cervical spine · treat raised pressure"] D -->|"9-13"| F["MODERATE
CT head + cervical spine"] D -->|"14-15"| G{"Any reason to go to hospital?
falling consciousness · severe vomiting

blocks.html:
• History: mechanism (young → motor vehicle crash · older → falls) · loss of consciousness · memory loss · medications and clotting problems
  • Physical exam: GCS · pupils (one fixed dilated pupil = third cranial nerve compressed) · posturing · signs of a skull-base fracture · other injuries
    • Decorticate (flexor) posturing: arms flexed to the "core" · damage above the red nucleus (hemispheres, internal capsule, thalamus, midbrain)
    • Decerebrate (extensor) posturing: arms and legs stiffly extended · brainstem below the red nucleus · worse
  • Investigations: CT head and cervical spine · consult other services for other injuries
  • Which minor injuries need a CT (the Canadian CT Head Rule) is not covered in either source - check the slides
2. Grading severity with the Glasgow Coma Scale
(sources differ: the upper-year GCS figure grades mild as 13-15 and moderate as 9-12 - check the slides)

• GCS is objective, reproducible and predicts outcome if scored within 6 hours · less reliable in infants and children, non-English speakers, and chronic conditions that impair speech or movement
  • Mortality in severe injury
    • GCS on admission: above 8 → 12% · 6-7 → 27% · 5 or less → 78% (sources differ: upper-year notes give 5-7 and under 5)
    • Epidural 10-25% vs subdural 45-70% · coma over a day 30-50% · intracranial pressure over 20 mmHg 50%
3. Types of head injury

• Skull fractures (open or closed)
    • linear (not displaced) · depressed (pushed inward onto the dura) · diastatic (along a suture)
    • Basilar: raccoon eyes · Battle sign (bruising behind the ear) · cerebrospinal fluid leaking from the nose or ear · blood behind an intact eardrum · may not show on CT · risk of meningitis
  • Focal injuries

rows: Between the skull and the stripped-off dura
Between the dura and the arachnoid
Middle meningeal artery (50%) torn by a fracture · 75-90% have a fracture
Contact: the head hits or is hit
Acceleration-deceleration, not impact · falls · often with diffuse axonal injury
Lucid interval, then coma · up to 40% start at GCS 14-15 · same-side blown pupil
Within 3 days · focal signs · chronic form common in the elderly
Surgery if symptomatic, over 1 cm, or a child
Usually surgery · within 4 hours ~30% mortality, after 4 hours ~90%

blocks.html:
• Contusion ("bruised brain"): coup under the impact · contrecoup on the opposite side · mixed high and low density on CT, usually several · large ones with mass effect are removed
  • traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage: frontal and temporal lobes · surgery if consciousness falls or there is a focal deficit
  • penetrating injury (knife, gunshot)
  • Diffuse injuries
    • concussion · traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage
    • diffuse axonal injury: shearing from rapid acceleration or deceleration · unconscious at the scene and stays in a coma · first CT often normal or tiny bleeds (corpus callosum, grey-white junction, pons) · in half of severe injuries

blocks.alt: epidural vs subdural hematoma - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Epidural vs subdural hematoma: arterial blood under the skull vs venous blood under the dura

blocks.html: 4. Raised intracranial pressure and herniation

• Swelling, vasodilation, vascular congestion and hematoma → ↑ intracranial pressure → poor brain perfusion + herniation
  • Presents as: falling consciousness · headache · vomiting · Cushing's triad (rising systolic pressure, slow heart rate, irregular breathing) · papilledema only after weeks
  • Treatment, one skull compartment at a time: blood (head of bed up, hyperventilate) · cerebrospinal fluid (drain it, make less) · brain tissue (remove the mass, mannitol) · plus airway protection if GCS is low · dexamethasone only helps swelling around a tumour

rows: Medial temporal lobe (uncus) over the tentorium
Same-side fixed dilated pupil (third nerve) · opposite-side weakness (cerebral peduncle) · drowsiness → coma
Diencephalon and midbrain down through the tentorium
Confusion, decorticate posturing · fixed mid-position pupils · diabetes insipidus · cortical blindness
Brain out through a fracture or surgical opening
Cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum

blocks.cap: Herniation: (a) subfalcine, (b) uncal, (c) central, (d) transcalvarial, (e) tonsillar

blocks.html: 5. Concussion

• Definition: a mild traumatic brain injury from rotational acceleration of the brain · 81-92% never lose consciousness · a blow to the chest can do it (whiplash) · helmets do not prevent it
    • diffuse injury without focal deficits (sources differ: the medwiki concussion note says "with focal neurologic deficits" - check the slides)
  • Risk factors: younger brain (longer recovery) · female (2:1, less neck muscle) · a previous concussion (less force needed, slower recovery) · poor sport technique · 65% are aged 5-18
  • Presents as: headache · dizziness · nausea · poor balance · "seeing stars" · memory and concentration problems ("brain fog")
  • Diagnosis: clinical - history and exam · no blood test, imaging or EEG confirms it
    • Concussion Recognition Tool for non-medical people on the field · Sport Concussion Assessment Tool for clinicians (one of 22 symptoms is enough; a child version for ages 5-12)
  • Treatment: "when in doubt, remove" from play, work or school · physical and mental rest for 24-48 hours (no screens, reading or schoolwork) but no extended rest · graded return over 1-4 weeks · school: part-time, easiest classes first, no gym
  • Outcome: most recover in 1-4 weeks · 15-30% still have symptoms after 4 weeks
    • complications: second-impact syndrome · post-concussion syndrome (over 2 weeks in adults, over 4 in youth) · post-traumatic epilepsy · depression and anxiety · chronic traumatic encephalopathy after repeated injuries

lectures.name: Multiple Sclerosis
lectures.title: Multiple sclerosis
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ MS needs lesions disseminated in time and space, with mimics excluded. A relapse is new, lasts over 24 hours, and has no other cause. Spinal cord ~50%, optic neuritis ~25%, brainstem ~15%. Oligoclonal bands are sensitive, not specific. Relapsing-remitting: 85%, young women; primary progressive: older, more men. Identical twins agree only 20-30% - mostly environment (EBV, smoking, low vitamin D).

blocks.html: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed by dissemination in time and space - lesions in different parts of the central nervous system at different times - once its mimics are excluded. A relapse is a new deficit lasting over 24 hours with no other cause.
1. What MS is

• Definition: immune-mediated (B and T cells) inflammation of the central nervous system that strips myelin - oligodendrocytes are damaged, and axons are lost over time
    • "multiple" = lesions in different places at different times · "sclerosis" = scars, so recovery is not always complete
  • Favoured sites: next to the cortex · around the ventricles · brainstem · cerebellum · spinal cord
  • Who: the most common disabling disease of the central nervous system in Canada (~240 per 100,000) · onset 20-40 · female 3:1 · Caucasian · more common further from the equator
  • Causes: genes plus environment
    • identical twins agree only 20-30% of the time
    • Epstein-Barr virus (past mononucleosis) · smoking · low vitamin D or sunlight · adolescent obesity · shift work · not coffee
    • immigrants to Canada take on the higher risk
2. Disease courses

rows: Attacks then recovery · incomplete recovery lets disability build
The long-term outcome of relapsing-remitting · steady worsening, occasional relapses

blocks.cap: Courses of multiple sclerosis: disability over time

blocks.html: 3. Relapses and how MS presents

• Relapse = a new neurological symptom · comes on over hours to days · lasts over 24 hours · not explained by another cause
  • Comparing a pseudorelapse with a new lesion is a lecture objective, but neither source covers it - check the slides
• Also: fatigue · cognitive change · depression and anxiety
4. Diagnosis

• Dissemination in time (more than one event) and space (more than one site) + other diseases excluded
  • MRI is the key test: lesions bright on T2/FLAIR, dark on T1
  • Lumbar puncture: oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid but not the blood · ~95% · sensitive, not specific
  • Disability is scored with the Expanded Disability Status Scale
  • Differential (once the MRI is done): neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder · myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein associated disease · acute disseminated encephalomyelitis · sarcoidosis · rheumatologic disease · tumour (lymphoma) · infection (HIV, Lyme, syphilis) · vitamin B12 deficiency

blocks.alt: multiple sclerosis lesions on T2 FLAIR and T1 MRI - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: MS lesions: bright periventricular spots on T2/FLAIR (left), dark holes on T1 (right)

blocks.html: 5. Treatment and outcome

• Corticosteroids (listed without detail in the upper-year notes)
  • Disease-modifying therapy (fewer relapses)
    • infusions: alemtuzumab · ocrelizumab · natalizumab
    • others: interferon beta · glatiramer acetate · ofatumumab · dimethyl fumarate · fingolimod · siponimod · ozanimod · teriflunomide · cladribine
    • (sources differ: the medwiki note's "oral" and "injectable" groups look swapped - check the slides for which is which)

• Experimental: fecal transplant (gut microbiome) · bone-marrow transplant
  • Outcome: 50% have minor disability by 6-8 years · 21% need a walking aid by 15 years

lectures.name: Approach to Stroke
lectures.title: Approach to stroke
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Non-contrast CT comes first, because any hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication to tPA. tPA within 4.5 hours; thrombectomy within 16-24 hours for a large-vessel occlusion with salvageable brain, whether or not tPA was given. Check glucose before calling it a stroke. Neglect or aphasia = cortex, not a lacune. Heart clot → anticoagulate; everything else → antiplatelet. Endarterectomy only for symptomatic stenosis over 70% on the stroke's side. Hypertensive bleeds are deep; amyloid bleeds are lobar.

blocks.html: Time is brain: rule out a mimic, image to exclude bleeding, then decide on clot-busting (tissue plasminogen activator, tPA, within 4.5 hours) and clot retrieval (thrombectomy, within 16-24 hours for a large-vessel occlusion). Once stable, the cause sets secondary prevention: a clot from the heart → anticoagulant; everything else → antiplatelet.
1. Hyperacute approach

flowchart TD A["Sudden focal deficit
paramedics activate the stroke protocol"] --> B["Point-of-care glucose (low sugar mimics stroke)
vitals · cardiac monitor · 2 IV lines
bloods: CBC, INR, creatinine, troponin

then CT angiogram + CT perfusion
goal: door to imaging under 25 min"] C --> D{"Hemorrhage?"} D -->|Yes| E["HEMORRHAGIC STROKE

and no contraindication?"} F -->|Yes| G["IV tPA
