blocks.html:
• Rule out mimics
    • hypoglycemia - check glucose first
    • migraine: weakness "marches" over minutes, slow onset and offset, crosses vascular territories, young women
    • Todd's paresis after a (maybe unwitnessed) seizure: improves over hours
    • psychogenic: inconsistent, improves with distraction, no vascular territory
    • hemorrhage: may not follow a territory, more often with headache
  • Localize before you look at the scan: you know where to look for subtle early changes and which vessels to study (suspected basilar clot → always a CT angiogram; a plain CT alone has missed basilar clots that ended in locked-in syndrome) · old infarcts and incidental findings will not distract you
2. Definitions and causes

• Stroke = sudden neurological deficit from a problem with the brain's blood supply
    • Ischemic (80-85%) = a blocked vessel · hemorrhagic = a ruptured vessel bleeding into or around the brain
    • transient ischemic attack (TIA) = symptoms usually under an hour and no infarct on CT or MRI
  • Penumbra = stunned but still living tissue around the dead core, fed by collaterals · salvageable if flow returns fast
  • Ischemic causes (the cause sets the treatment)
    • artery to artery: carotid, intracranial stenosis, aorta · cardioembolic · small-vessel (lacunar) · artery dissection · low perfusion → watershed infarcts between territories · cryptogenic (~25%)

blocks.cap: Ischemic core and penumbra on CT

blocks.html: 3. Stroke syndromes

rows: Aphasia + right face and arm > leg weakness
Left neglect · anosognosia + left face and arm > leg weakness
Pure motor · pure sensory · ataxic hemiparesis · sensorimotor · clumsy hand-dysarthria · no cortical signs
Vertigo · eye-movement weakness · crossed face and body findings · cranial nerve signs · both sides weak

blocks.html: • Neglect or aphasia = cortex, so a middle cerebral artery stroke, not a lacune
4. Imaging

• Non-contrast CT: rules out hemorrhage (absolute contraindication to tPA) · shows early ischemic change = dead brain (dark, loss of grey-white difference) · more dead brain → more bleeding with tPA · over a third of the middle cerebral artery territory → no tPA
  • CT angiogram: finds a large-vessel occlusion · CT perfusion: a mismatch = brain that can still be saved

blocks.cap: Early ischemic change on CT: an acute infarct beside normal brain

blocks.html: 5. Thrombolysis with tPA

• Turns plasminogen into plasmin, which breaks down clot · up to 4.5 hours from onset, earlier is better · number needed to treat 7.7
  • 0.9 mg/kg: 10% as a bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 1 hour
  • Risk: significant bleeding 6% - vessels beyond the clot are damaged, and burst when flow returns (hemorrhagic transformation)
  • Only 10-20% qualify: too late · unwitnessed onset · anticoagulated or other risk · too mild · hemorrhagic
  • Contraindications
    • any hemorrhage on CT, or a past intracerebral hemorrhage · large early ischemic change · symptoms of subarachnoid hemorrhage · seizure at onset
    • BP over 185/110 despite treatment (sources differ: the medwiki note says 185/100 - check the slides)
    • stroke or serious head injury under 3 months · major surgery under 14 days · gastrointestinal or urinary bleed under 21 days · arterial puncture at a site you cannot compress, or a lumbar puncture, under 7 days
    • platelets under 100 · INR over 1.4 or PTT over 40 s (sources differ: the medwiki note says INR "< 1.4") · factor Xa inhibitor in the last 24-48 h (sources differ: the medwiki note says "xanthine oxidase inhibitors")
    • glucose under 3 or over 22 · caution in pregnancy, pericarditis, endocarditis (listen to the heart first)
6. Thrombectomy

• Under 5% qualify: proximal large-artery occlusion (internal carotid, middle cerebral M1/M2) · disabling stroke · penumbra on perfusion · under 16-24 hours from onset or last seen well · not lacunar (cannot be reached)
  • Can be given even when tPA was not · a catheter carries a stent retriever that grabs the clot

blocks.alt: mechanical thrombectomy stent retriever - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Thrombectomy: a stent retriever pulls the clot out and restores flow

blocks.html: 7. Stroke unit and finding the cause

• Admission orders: close BP watch for 24 h (high pressure is common and settles in 2-7 days - do not lower it unless very high) · repeat imaging at 24 h for bleeding · nothing by mouth until a swallowing assessment · bed rest 24 h · physiotherapy, occupational therapy, social work
  • No bleed at 24 h → start ASA, clot prevention in the legs, and a statin · intensive rehabilitation beats even tPA (most recovery in 3 months, some up to a year)
  • Look for the cause
    • anterior circulation → carotid imaging · posterior circulation → vertebral and basilar imaging only
    • heart: echocardiogram (transthoracic, transesophageal, bubble study for a patent foramen ovale) · telemetry or Holter monitor for atrial fibrillation
    • atherosclerosis risk: glucose and HbA1c · lipids · BP
8. Secondary prevention

rows: Anticoagulant: warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant, ~2 weeks after the stroke
Antiplatelet: ASA 81 mg · clopidogrel if ASA fails · both for some high-risk patients
Symptomatic carotid stenosis over 70% (same side as the stroke)
carotid endarterectomy or stenting · not for stenosis on the other side

blocks.html:
• Plus BP under 140/90 · glucose control · high-dose statin · exercise, diet, smoking cessation
  • Risk factors beyond heart disease: pregnancy and postpartum · cocaine or amphetamines (vasospasm) · bleeding disorders and anticoagulants (hemorrhage)
9. Transient ischemic attack

• Brief symptoms that resolve completely
  • CT head to exclude mimics (subdural hematoma, tumour) · start ASA (already on ASA → add clopidogrel for 21 days) · ECG if the pulse is irregular · refer to a rapid TIA clinic (echocardiogram, Holter, CT angiogram or carotid Doppler, lipids, glucose, BP) · then manage as secondary prevention
  • Crescendo TIAs (several in a day or two) → admit urgently: very high stroke risk
10. Hemorrhagic stroke

• Intracerebral hemorrhage causes
    • hypertensive arteriopathy → deep bleeds (pons, basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum)
    • Amyloid (congophilic) angiopathy → lobar bleeds just under the cortex
    • tumour (usually metastasis) · arteriovenous malformation · cavernoma · aneurysm · clotting disorder
  • Treatment: BP under 160/110 · hold all antiplatelets and anticoagulants · compression devices for the legs, heparin only after a stable 24-hour CT · MRI or CT angiogram for the cause · surgery rarely (only an accessible clot raising pressure) · rehabilitation
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage: thunderclap headache · usually a ruptured aneurysm · neurosurgery (coiling or clipping) · risks: re-bleeding, vasospasm, pneumonia

lectures.name: Approach to Sensory Symptoms
lectures.title: Approach to sensory symptoms
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Polyneuropathy starts in the toes and reaches the fingertips when it reaches the knees. Guillain-Barré = weakness ascending over days with lost reflexes; watch the breathing. A sensory level with brisk reflexes below it is the spinal cord. Root: dermatome, fuzzy borders, whole-myotome weakness; nerve: sharp borders, only that nerve's muscles. Demyelination recovers in weeks; axons regrow over months to years.

blocks.html: Localize first - the shape of the sensory loss says where the lesion is. Half the body = brain · a level on the trunk = spinal cord · one dermatome = root · one nerve with sharp borders = mononeuropathy · toes first, then fingertips = length-dependent polyneuropathy.
1. Localizing sensory symptoms

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["Numbness, tingling or pain"] --> B{"Where is it?"} B -->|"One side of the face and body"| C["BRAIN (e.g. thalamus)
± visual, motor, coordination signs
later: central pain on that side"] B -->|"Everything below a level on the trunk
± bladder urgency, brisk reflexes below"| D["SPINAL CORD
(myelopathy)"] B -->|"One dermatome + neck or back pain
radiating down a limb, fuzzy borders"| E["NERVE ROOT
(radiculopathy)"] B -->|"One named nerve, sharp borders"| F["MONONEUROPATHY
e.g. carpal tunnel, peroneal nerve"] B -->|"Both feet first, rising symmetrically"| G{"Tempo and main deficit?"} G -->|"Months to years
mostly sensory, burning"| H["LENGTH-DEPENDENT POLYNEUROPATHY
e.g. diabetic"] G -->|"Days
mostly weakness, reflexes lost"| I["GUILLAIN-BARRÉ SYNDROME"]

blocks.html:
• Characterize the neuropathy - the differential is long, so narrow it four ways
    • modality: sensory · motor · autonomic
    • time course: acute (1 day-6 weeks) · subacute (6 weeks-6 months) · chronic (over 6 months)
    • distribution: length-dependent polyneuropathy · mononeuropathy · mononeuritis multiplex
    • damage: axonal vs demyelinating - best shown by nerve conduction studies and electromyography (EMG)
  • Cord vs nerve: sensory loss on the trunk points to the cord · bladder trouble suggests the cord but is not specific · symmetry and back pain do not help
  • Romberg sign is positive with: both S1 roots · a length-dependent sensory neuropathy · dorsal column disease
2. Root or single nerve?

rows: Root squeezed in its foramen ("pinched nerve")
Compression at a common site (e.g. the carpal tunnel)
Neck or back pain + electric or burning pain down the limb · worse with some positions (neck extension)
Numbness, tingling, maybe burning · worse with leaning, driving, typing
Every muscle of that root + reflex loss

blocks.html:
• Weak thumb abduction: C8 root → medial hand and forearm numb + other C8 muscles weak · median nerve → thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger numb + only median muscles weak
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome (most common): median-territory tingling, worse at night, better with shaking · night splints, steroid injection, surgical release · can be confused with a C6 root
  • Foot drop from the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck: weak dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion · numb top of the foot · reflexes intact
  • S1 root: low back pain · numb little toe and sole · absent ankle reflex
3. Four kinds of peripheral nerve damage

rows: Local anesthetic (lidocaine) · cold · brief compression · neurapraxia
Regrows ~1-2 mm a day (upper-year notes: about an inch a month) · months to years · unlikely after 2 years
Far end of the longest axons first
Metabolic: diabetes, kidney failure · drugs: vincristine, cisplatin, metronidazole · heavy metals: lead, arsenic, mercury
Slow, incomplete, only if the cause is removed
Myelin over one or more internodes → signal fails
Immune: Guillain-Barré syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy · diphtheria toxin · hereditary: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
Cell body: anterior horn or dorsal root ganglion
Motor: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, polio, West Nile · sensory: cisplatin, paraneoplastic, Sjögren, vitamin B6 toxicity

blocks.cap: Where neuropathy causes act: systemic causes everywhere, root and plexus causes proximally, compression and trauma distally

blocks.html: 4. Three bilateral patterns to tell apart

rows: Stocking and glove: toes → feet → ankles → knees, then fingertips
Brisk below the level · spastic (upper motor neuron)
Autonomic failure when severe: low BP on standing, bladder, constipation
Cranial nerves and breathing muscles → respiratory failure
Bladder urgency · poor balance, falls, wide gait
Treat the pain (analgesic, antidepressant) · sugar control will not reverse it
MRI of the cord (and head if multiple sclerosis is possible)

blocks.html:
• Why toes first: axonal transport fails over distance, so the longest axons (to the toes, from S1) go first · the knee-to-spine distance matches fingertip-to-neck, so the hands start when the legs reach the knees
  • Diabetic neuropathy = the most common neuropathy in Canada · symmetric, sensory first, painful · shooting pain down a leg is a root, not diabetes
  • Guillain-Barré = acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy: autoimmune, antibody-mediated

blocks.cap: Stocking-and-glove distribution of a length-dependent polyneuropathy

lectures.name: Neuropathic Pain
lectures.title: Neuropathic pain
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Allodynia = pain from a non-painful touch; hyperpathia = too much pain from a painful one. Trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine; postherpetic neuralgia → gabapentin. One drug at a time, titrated to the maximum - switch only for side effects or no effect after a month at the top dose. Opioids are the last resort. Complex regional pain syndrome: more pain, for longer, than the injury explains, with autonomic features.

blocks.html: Neuropathic pain comes from a damaged or malfunctioning nervous system, not from injured tissue - so it is treated differently from ordinary (nociceptive) pain. Recognize it by its symptoms, find the cause, then trial one drug at a time, titrated slowly to the maximum dose.
1. Two kinds of pain

rows: Lesion or dysfunction of the nervous system itself

blocks.html: 2. Symptoms

• Allodynia = pain from something that should not hurt (clothes, bedsheets)
  • Hyperpathia = an exaggerated response to something that should hurt (a pinprick is agonizing)
  • Dysesthesia = unpleasant abnormal sensations
    • numbness or tingling (paresthesia) · burning · electric shocks or shooting pain (neuralgia)
3. Causes

rows: Lesions of the thalamus, brainstem or spinal cord
A focal tissue or nerve injury → chronic pain greater and longer than the injury explains
Postherpetic neuralgia · trigeminal neuralgia · nerve injury

blocks.html: 4. Treatment

blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["Neuropathic pain confirmed"] --> B{"A classic syndrome?"} B -->|"Trigeminal neuralgia"| C["CARBAMAZEPINE"] B -->|"Postherpetic neuralgia"| D["GABAPENTIN"] B -->|"Other"| E["Pick one agent to fit co-existing problems
(sleep, depression)"] E --> F["Titrate up slowly to the maximum dose"] F --> G{"Side effects before benefit?
Or no benefit after 1 month at the top dose?"} G -->|Yes| H["SWITCH to another agent"] G -->|No| I["Continue"] H --> F

rows: Carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia · gabapentin for postherpetic neuralgia
Capsaicin (hot-pepper gel, 3 times a day) · lidocaine gel or patch
Opioids only as a last resort - they rarely help much

blocks.html:
• The choice depends on what else the patient has (poor sleep → amitriptyline · depression → duloxetine)
  • Treating neuropathic pain is not the same as treating nociceptive pain

lectures.name: Approach to Headache
lectures.title: Approach to headache
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Screen every headache for red flags first: a thunderclap headache is a subarachnoid hemorrhage until an early CT - and a lumbar puncture if the CT is negative - says otherwise. Over 50 with jaw claudication → ESR and steroids before the biopsy. Raised pressure is worse lying and on waking; a CSF leak is better lying. Tension-type: both sides, pressing, no nausea; migraine: one side, throbbing, worse with activity. Migraine patients lie still; cluster patients pace. Triptans at onset, not with coronary disease; acute drugs under 10 days a month.

blocks.html: First ask whether this is a secondary headache: screen every headache for red flags, because the rare secondary causes kill or disable. With no red flags it is a primary headache (about 90%), and duration, side, quality and behaviour during the attack name it: migraine, tension-type or cluster.
1. The approach

xanthochromia if CT is negative"] C -->|"Over 50, jaw claudication,
scalp tenderness"| E["GIANT CELL ARTERITIS?
ESR · steroids at once · biopsy"] C -->|"Fever, stiff neck"| F["MENINGITIS?
CT if raised pressure · lumbar puncture
empiric antibiotics"] C -->|"Focal signs, papilledema,
worse on waking or lying down"| G["MASS or RAISED PRESSURE?
CT or MRI"] C -->|"None"| H{"PRIMARY HEADACHE
which pattern?"} H -->|"4-72 h, one side, throbbing,
nausea, light and sound sensitivity,
lies still"| I["MIGRAINE"] H -->|"30 min-7 days, both sides,

blocks.html:
• Brain tissue has no pain receptors - the pain comes from what surrounds it (periosteum, dural and scalp arteries, veins, cranial nerves V, VII, IX, X, neck muscles, eyes, ears, sinuses, scalp)
  • History: onset (worst ever? instantaneous? new after 50?) · wakes from sleep or worse on waking → raised pressure · worse with cough or position · associated features · hormonal status (pregnancy, contraceptive pill, hormone therapy)
  • Exam: vitals · temporal arteries · pupils and visual fields · fundoscopy for papilledema · neck flexion · neurological exam
2. Red flags and what they mean

rows: Systemic illness (cancer, HIV, fever, stiff neck, rash)
Focal neurological signs (other than a typical aura)
Cerebral venous thrombosis · carotid dissection · pituitary apoplexy
Mass · idiopathic intracranial hypertension · encephalitis, meningitis

blocks.html: 3. Secondary headaches

rows: Thunderclap: worst ever, peaks in seconds
CT early (sensitivity falls each day) → lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if negative
Worse on waking or lying · sleepy · blurred vision · ↓ consciousness · Cushing's triad
Obesity, contraceptive pill, steroids, vitamin A, tetracycline · pulsatile ringing in the ears · horizontal double vision · brief visual blackouts · papilledema
Weight loss · acetazolamide or topiramate · shunt or optic nerve sheath fenestration
Better lying, worse upright · after lumbar puncture or surgery, or spontaneous
Over 50 · jaw claudication · scalp tenderness · visual symptoms · polymyalgia, fever, sweats · tender nodular temporal artery
High-dose prednisone (60-100 mg) as soon as suspected, taper as ESR settles · untreated → blindness or stroke
One-sided headache spreading to the neck and face · Horner syndrome · stroke risk
ASA (clopidogrel if it fails) · anticoagulation in hospital · stenting
Steady, worse in the morning, ± vomiting · worse with cough or position · resists usual remedies
Fever + stiff neck · Kernig and Brudzinski signs
CT if raised pressure · lumbar puncture · blood cultures

blocks.cap: Raised intracranial pressure causes the Cushing reflex: hypertension, bradycardia, respiratory suppression

blocks.html: 4. Migraine

• Features: one-sided, throbbing, disabling · 4-72 hours · nausea or vomiting · light and sound sensitivity · women over 75%
    • central sensitization in over 80% → allodynia (brushing hair or wearing glasses hurts)
    • aura in 15-20%: usually visual, typically under 30 min, spreads gradually · 3-5% have aura without headache
  • Diagnosis
    • without aura: at least 5 attacks of 4-72 h + 2 of one-sided · pulsating · moderate-severe · worse with routine activity + 1 of nausea or vomiting · light and sound sensitivity
    • with aura: at least 2 attacks with a spreading aura (each symptom 5-60 min) followed within 60 min by headache
  • Migraine aura vs TIA: positive symptoms (sparkles) vs visual loss · gradual and sequential vs abrupt and simultaneous · up to 60 min vs under 15 · headache follows about half vs rarely
  • Acute treatment - treat early in the attack, no imaging needed
    • NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac) · avoid with a gastrointestinal bleed, ulcer, kidney disease, pregnancy, bleeding disorder
    • Triptans (serotonin agonists: constrict vessels, ↓ CGRP release) · best at onset, not as a last resort · side effects: chest or jaw tightness, flushing, nausea · avoid in coronary, cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, Raynaud
    • gepants · antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) · avoid opioids
    • limit acute drugs to under 10 days a month to prevent medication overuse headache (sources differ: the medwiki note says 10-15 times a month, or 2-3 days a week - check the slides)
  • Prevention
    • when: disabling attacks despite acute treatment · 4 or more attacks a month · acute drugs fail or cannot be used · overuse risk · frequent or long auras
    • lifestyle (SEEDS): Sleep · Exercise · Eat well · Diary of triggers · Stress
    • success = 50% fewer attacks · start low, go slow · try tapering after 6-9 months of remission

rows: First preventive · caution in childbearing age · constipation, injection-site reaction
Has hypertension · low BP · avoid in heart failure, asthma, diabetes
Fewest side effects · caution in childbearing age
Co-existing anxiety or depression · drowsiness, weight gain, dry mouth
No longer strongly recommended (2024) · weight loss, tingling, acidosis

blocks.cap: Phases of a migraine attack: triggers, prodrome, aura, headache, postdrome

blocks.html: 5. Tension-type headache and cluster headache

• Tension-type: the most common headache (~38% a year) · onset ~25-30 · no imaging needed
    • acute: acetaminophen · ibuprofen · naproxen · prevent: amitriptyline first line · mirtazapine · venlafaxine · tizanidine · triptans and onabotulinumtoxinA do not work
  • Cluster headache (a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia): rare (0.1%) · onset ~30 · men 3:1 · smokers · severe one-sided pain around the eye · cannot stay still (unlike migraine) · predictable timing · hypothalamus · MRI
    • acute: sumatriptan 6 mg under the skin · zolmitriptan nasal · 100% oxygen, 12-15 L/min for 15 min
    • bridge: steroids · dihydroergotamine · nerve blocks · prevent: verapamil (ECG monitoring) · galcanezumab · lithium rarely

lectures.name: Approach to Altered Level of Consciousness
lectures.title: Approach to altered level of consciousness
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Vegetative state is awake but not aware; locked-in syndrome is aware but cannot move - only the eyes and blink are left. Rule out the treatable causes (sugar, shock, drugs, infection, hematoma) before labelling a coma. Coma needs both hemispheres, both thalami, or the brainstem above the mid-pons. The gag/cough reflex is usually the last to go. The FOUR score works in an intubated patient; the GCS verbal score does not. Brain death = no brainstem reflexes + no breathing + no confounders.

blocks.html: Consciousness has two parts - being awake (alertness) and knowing it (awareness) - and the approach is about which part is lost, and why. First fix what is treatable, then examine the brainstem reflexes to place the patient on the spectrum from coma to brain death.
1. The approach to a patient with reduced responsiveness
2. What keeps us conscious

• Alertness (arousal): wakefulness · vigilance · responding to stimuli
  • Awareness (content): everything the cortex does - sensation, attention, memory, executive function
  • Both are maintained by the ascending reticular activating system
    • the reticular formation in the upper pons and midbrain → projects widely through the thalamus (intralaminar nuclei) and hypothalamus → cerebral cortex

blocks.alt: ascending reticular activating system - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Ascending reticular activating system: reticular formation in the upper pons and midbrain projecting through both thalami to the cortex

blocks.html: 3. Causes of altered consciousness

• Coma = complete loss of alertness and awareness · the system fails at one of three places:
    • both hemispheres (global cortical): metabolic, toxic, hypoxic-ischemic, trauma, large bilateral lesions
    • both thalami or the hypothalamus: stroke, destructive lesions, tumour
    • brainstem above the mid-pons: trauma, stroke, herniation
  • Other causes of an altered level of consciousness: syncope · seizure · encephalopathy or delirium
    • delirium: inattention, perseveration, distractibility · fluctuates, worse at night · disrupted sleep-wake cycle · hallucinations, delusions, agitation · sometimes autonomic overactivity and tremor
  • Coma mimics (aware and alert but cannot show it): locked-in syndrome · severe neuromuscular disease (Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis) · neuromuscular blockade · akinetic mutism · psychogenic unresponsiveness
4. Examining the unconscious patient

• Observe: how much stimulation it takes to get a response · agitation · any communication · breathing pattern · spontaneous or asymmetric movement · yawning, sneezing, coughing, swallowing · fundoscopy for papilledema
  • Cranial nerve reflexes

rows: "Blown" dilated pupil = third nerve lost · a small pupil = sympathetic loss (Horner's syndrome)
Only if the cervical spine is cleared
Cold water: in coma the eyes drift slowly toward the cold ear with no fast phase
Eyelids close (sources differ: medwiki says use saline to avoid abrasion, upper-year notes say cotton - check the slides)
Suction catheter down the breathing tube · often the last reflex lost

blocks.html:
• Motor: tone · spontaneous movement · response to pain (central: sternal rub, trapezius squeeze, supraorbital pressure · peripheral: nail bed) · is it reproducible, not just a reflex? · reflexes and Babinski sign
    • posturing: decorticate (flexor) · decerebrate (extensor) · triple flexion = a spinal reflex, needs no brainstem
  • Coma scales: Glasgow Coma Scale (built for head injury; verbal score impossible if intubated) · FOUR score (eyes, motor, brainstem reflexes, breathing - no verbal part, so it works when intubated)
5. Disorders of consciousness

rows: Cranial nerve reflexes kept · reflex responses to pain · does not track with the eyes, no communication · loses bowel and bladder control
Visual pursuit · localizes pain · appropriate smiling or crying
Functional communication and use of objects
Cannot speak or move except the eyes and blinking (third nerve spared)

blocks.cap: Disorders of consciousness: coma, unresponsive wakefulness, minimally conscious minus and plus, emergence; locked-in syndrome off to the side

blocks.html: 6. Brain death

• All of: a deep, unresponsive coma with no motor response on either side (spinal reflexes allowed) · no brainstem reflexes (gag, cough, corneal, pupillary, vestibulo-ocular) · no breathing effort on the apnea test · no confounding condition that could mimic it
  • Canadian guideline: a brain-based definition of death (2023)

blocks.cap: Consciousness on two axes: arousal against awareness, with brain death, coma, vegetative state and minimally conscious state at the bottom left

lectures.name: Approach to Seizures
lectures.title: Approach to seizures
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A single unprovoked seizure with a normal MRI and EEG is usually not treated (recurrence under 60%); a lesion, epileptiform discharges or a second unprovoked seizure makes it epilepsy, and treatment is recommended. Provoked seizure → fix the cause, no drug. Aura, asymmetric onset or a post-ictal deficit → focal → image the brain. Epilepsy = 2 unprovoked seizures over 24 hours apart. Drug-resistant = 2 appropriate drugs failed → epilepsy centre.

blocks.html: After a first seizure the questions come in order: was it really a seizure, was it provoked, and how likely is another? The whole workup exists to estimate that last number - a recurrence risk of 60% or more is epilepsy, and that is when an antiseizure drug starts.
1. Seizure, epilepsy and how seizures are classified

• Seizure = a transient episode of signs or symptoms from abnormally excessive or synchronous neuronal activity
  • Epilepsy = an enduring predisposition to seizures (criteria in section 5)
  • Classified by where it starts (International League Against Epilepsy)
    • Focal: one area of the brain → localizable symptoms · aware (old "simple partial") or impaired awareness (old "complex partial") · motor or non-motor · can spread to a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
    • Generalized: the whole brain from the start · motor: tonic-clonic (most common), tonic, clonic, atonic, myoclonic · non-motor: absence (specific changes on the electroencephalogram, EEG)
    • unknown onset: unwitnessed or unclear
  • Why classify: focal seizures usually mean a brain lesion → imaging is required · primary generalized epilepsy has no focal lesion, so imaging is usually not needed · the type also guides the drug choice
  • Clues that it was focal: an aura (rising epigastric feeling, déjà vu, forced memories) · asymmetric onset · deficits afterwards (postictal Todd's paresis) · cortical signs: language problems, pronator drift, reflex asymmetry, weakness, visual field defect

blocks.alt: focal vs. generalized vs. unkown onset seizures.png
blocks.cap: Focal (60% of epilepsy), generalized (30%) and unknown onset (10%), with their secondary classifications

blocks.html: 2. The approach to a first seizure

• History is the key test
    • the event: details of the onset, the rest of the seizure and the post-ictal state · in a true seizure the eyes are fixed, not roving side to side (unlike a psychogenic event)
    • earlier events recognised only in hindsight (auras, staring spells) - these may mean it is not the first
    • risk factors: febrile seizures or childhood epilepsy · significant head trauma · past meningitis or encephalitis · family history
  • Physical exam is often normal · look for tongue biting and injuries · ongoing confusion or a focal deficit is a red flag
3. Provoked vs unprovoked

rows: A transient factor lowers the threshold of an otherwise normal brain
Genetic conditions · old stroke, old trauma, brain tumour · neurocysticercosis scar
Higher - the brain itself is the problem

blocks.html: 4. Investigations

• Their job is to estimate the risk of recurrence
  • Bloodwork guided by the history · electrolytes always
  • Imaging: CT acutely in the emergency department · MRI is part of every first-seizure workup (look closely at the temporal lobes) · a structural lesion raises the recurrence risk
  • EEG is required · epileptiform discharges raise the recurrence risk
5. When to start a drug, and epilepsy

• Epilepsy is diagnosed by any one of:
    • 2 unprovoked (or reflex) seizures more than 24 hours apart
    • 1 unprovoked seizure + a recurrence risk of at least 60% over 10 years (a lesion on MRI, discharges on EEG)
    • an epilepsy syndrome
  • Causes: structural (stroke, trauma, tumour, mesial temporal sclerosis, developmental) · genetic · infectious (viral encephalitis, bacterial meningitis, neurocysticercosis) · metabolic (inborn errors) · immune (autoimmune, paraneoplastic)
  • Syndromes = a set pattern of seizure types, EEG, age of onset and course: childhood absence epilepsy · juvenile myoclonic epilepsy · benign Rolandic epilepsy · West syndrome · Dravet syndrome · Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
  • Comorbidities: non-epileptic seizures · depression, anxiety · attention deficit · migraine · cognitive impairment · sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP)

blocks.cap: Unprovoked first seizure: discharges, a remote symptomatic cause or an epileptogenic lesion put the patient at intermediate or high risk

blocks.html: 6. Long-term management

• Antiseizure drugs either take the foot off the gas (less firing) or add a brake (more GABA)
  • Choosing: one drug vs several · treats a comorbidity too (headache, mood)? · side effects · adherence · levels, titration, switching · drug interactions · cost · pregnancy: teratogenicity
  • Drug-resistant epilepsy = 2 appropriate, tolerated drugs have failed → refer to an epilepsy centre
    • continuous video-EEG to characterize the seizures · psychological testing · intracranial EEG
    • surgery: resect the mesial temporal lobe · responsive neurostimulation · vagus nerve stimulation

lectures.name: Recovery in the Nervous System
lectures.title: Recovery in the nervous system
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Central axons can regrow inside a peripheral nerve graft - so it is the central environment, not the neuron, that blocks regeneration. Peripheral regrowth needs a nearby stump, an intact Schwann cell tube, a clean cut and no ischemia or infection. Crush injury → traumatic neuroma. Facial nerve regrowth gone wrong → synkinesis, including tears while eating.

blocks.html: A cut axon always loses its far end; whether it grows back depends on where it is. Peripheral axons can regrow along an empty Schwann cell tube if the conditions are right; central axons are held back by their surroundings, not by an inability to grow.
1. What happens when an axon is cut

• Beyond the cut (distal): Wallerian degeneration - the axon degenerates and is cleared
    • starts days after the injury · the cytoskeleton breaks down, the membrane fails · macrophages eat the debris · myelin breaks into "ovoids"
  • Before the cut (proximal): the stump and cell body swell · the cell body loses its Nissl substance (central chromatolysis) · the axon starts to sprout as it tries to regrow
  • Support: Schwann cells multiply, clear debris and release growth factors and cytokines · the cell body releases trophic factors
  • Damage can spread across synapses to the neurons upstream and downstream (trans-synaptic degeneration)
  • How the injury is graded (neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis) and how strength returns in steps: see 03 - Nerve Injury

blocks.cap: After a cut: Wallerian degeneration of the distal axon, macrophages and Schwann cells clear the debris, then the axon regrows and is remyelinated

blocks.html: 2. Peripheral vs central regeneration

rows: Sprouts grow from the proximal stump along the empty distal Schwann cell tube
Laminin, nerve growth factor and other factors from Schwann cells
Central axons regrow into a peripheral nerve graft → the problem is the central environment, not the neuron
Plasticity (other circuits taking over) may matter more than regrowth

blocks.html: 3. Conditions for successful peripheral regeneration

• The stumps are close - the proximal stump must reach the distal Schwann cell tube (stump-to-stump contact)
  • An intact tube to follow (endoneurium preserved) - without one, regrowth goes off course
  • A clean cut rather than a crush or a mangling injury
  • No complications - no ischemia, no infection
4. When regeneration goes wrong

• Misguided, haphazard sprouting reaches the wrong target
  • Synkinesis: moving one muscle involuntarily moves another
    • common after facial nerve injury (muscles of facial expression) and in the extraocular muscles
    • salivary fibres rewired to the lacrimal gland → tears while eating
  • Traumatic neuroma: the perineurium is torn, so regrowing axons escape and branch in a tangle
    • more likely after crush or mangling injury than a clean cut · can cause chronic pain
    • Morton's neuroma is a related example (more collagen and mixed tissue)

lectures.name: Neurosurgical Emergencies
lectures.title: Neurosurgical emergencies
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Mannitol shrinks brain with an intact blood-brain barrier; dexamethasone shrinks the swelling around a tumour by restoring a broken one. Epidural: lens, arterial, lucid interval - operate if symptomatic, over 1 cm or a child. Subdural: crescent, bridging veins, slower. A ruptured aneurysm must be secured or it re-bleeds. Hydrocephalus: drain now (external ventricular drain), shunt later. Saddle anesthesia + bladder or bowel loss = cauda equina emergency. No steroids for an abscess.

blocks.html: Most neurosurgical emergencies come down to raised intracranial pressure: something is taking up space inside a closed skull. The decision is what that something is - blood, tumour, swollen brain or trapped cerebrospinal fluid - because each is removed or shrunk a different way. Head injury grading, Glasgow Coma Scale scoring and the herniation types are in 01 - Approach to Head Injuries.
1. Does this patient need a neurosurgeon?

• The exam: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) · cranial nerves (pupils) · motor: pronator drift, bulk, tone, power, reflexes · sensory: light touch, pinprick, proprioception · cerebellar exam not essential
  • Imaging: identify the lesion - hematoma, hemorrhage, mass, enlarged ventricles
2. Raised intracranial pressure

• Normal: 7-20 cm water (5-15 mmHg) in adults · lower in children (3-7) and infants (1.5-6)
  • Fixed box: brain + cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) + blood + any mass = a fixed volume · the skull first compensates by pushing out venous blood and CSF, then pressure rises steeply once a critical volume is passed
  • Causes
    • focal: tumour · hemorrhage (spontaneous or traumatic) · abscess · infarct
    • generalized: hydrocephalus · meningitis or encephalitis · brain swelling (edema)
  • Presents as: falling consciousness · headache and vomiting · Cushing's triad (rising systolic pressure, slow heart rate, irregular breathing) · papilledema only late · herniation (third nerve palsy most common; posterior cerebral artery infarct)
    • the raised-pressure headache is a major red flag: persistent, progressive, worse lying down, in the morning, and with coughing or straining
  • Measuring it: lumbar puncture (risky if there is a mass - may cause herniation) or an intracranial monitor, with or without a ventricular drain
3. Lowering the pressure: what is taking up the space?

• Mannitol vs dexamethasone: mannitol needs an intact barrier to draw water out · dexamethasone repairs a broken barrier around a tumour
  • Craniotomy: the clot is thick and jelly-like, so it cannot simply be suctioned out through a burr hole (sources differ: upper-year notes list "burr holes or craniotomy" for an epidural hematoma - check the slides)
  • CSF production can also be reduced with a diuretic (furosemide)
4. The acute bleeds: which one, and what to do

Surgery if symptomatic, over 1 cm, or a child · only very small ones watched

The aneurysm must be treated - high risk of re-rupture · don't drop the blood pressure too far early, but very high pressure risks a rebleed
Surgery if consciousness falls or there is a focal deficit

blocks.cap: CT: epidural hematoma is lens-shaped (convex), subdural hematoma is a crescent

blocks.html: 5. Masses on brain imaging

• Tumour: contrast-enhanced MRI is best (contrast CT if MRI unavailable) · enhancement suggests a high-grade tumour · surrounding swelling → dexamethasone
    • metastases (the most common brain tumours): multiple, ring-enhancing, with swelling around them · usually from lung, breast, melanoma, kidney
  • Brain abscess: think of it with fever · lumbar puncture is low-yield (no organism in over 80%) and can be harmful with a mass · surgery; no role for steroids

blocks.cap: Contrast MRI: multiple ring-enhancing lesions, typical of metastases

blocks.html: 6. Hydrocephalus

• Hydrocephalus = CSF builds up in the ventricles → compresses the brain from the inside → ↑ pressure
  • Can kill if untreated · acutely an external ventricular drain, long term a shunt
  • Complication named in the sources: shunt infection (a risk factor for meningitis) · other shunt complications are not covered in either source - check the slides
7. Spinal emergencies

blocks.html:
• Cord compression: thoracic lesions give upper motor neuron signs in both legs, a sensory level and possible bladder and bowel loss · complete injury = no rectal tone and no perianal sensation · cord syndromes: see 08 - Spinal Cord
  • Cauda equina: roots below the cord (cord ends at L1) · both legs, saddle anesthesia, loss of bowel or bladder control, lower motor neuron weakness
  • Management here (MRI, dexamethasone, surgery within 48 hours) comes from the medwiki condition notes, not the lecture note or the upper-year notes - check the slides

lectures.name: Neuroinfections
lectures.title: Neuroinfections
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Never delay antibiotics for the CT or the lumbar puncture - cultures, then empiric treatment (ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone in adults), and the CT only decides whether the tap is safe. Add ampicillin for Listeria in the elderly or immunocompromised; add acyclovir for seizures or focal signs. Neutrophils + low glucose = bacterial; lymphocytes + normal glucose = viral. Temporal lobe signs + red cells in the CSF → herpes encephalitis, confirmed by CSF PCR. Neonates: E. coli and group B strep - cefotaxime or gentamicin with ampicillin.

blocks.html: Suspected bacterial meningitis is a race: blood cultures, then antibiotics - never held back for the CT or the lumbar puncture. The CT only decides whether a lumbar puncture is safe; the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) then tells bacterial from viral, and seizures, confusion or focal signs point to herpes encephalitis.
1. Infections of the central nervous system

• Four kinds of organism: bacterial (bacterial meningitis, abscess) · viral (viral meningitis, viral encephalitis) · fungal (cryptococcus) · protozoal / parasitic (neurocysticercosis)
  • Four places it can sit: meningitis (the meninges) · encephalitis (the brain tissue) · meningoencephalitis (meninges, then brain) · brain abscess (walled off in a capsule)
  • Bacterial meningitis is the one not to miss

blocks.cap: Meningitis, encephalitis, meningoencephalitis and abscess: where in the brain each infection sits

blocks.html: 2. Bacterial meningitis: how it presents

• Classic triad: fever · stiff neck (nuchal rigidity) · altered mental status - 95% have at least 2 of the 3, so think of it with any one
  • Adults: a preceding viral illness · looks very sick · headache · seizures · light sensitivity · nausea and vomiting · fever (may be absent in the elderly) · non-blanching meningococcal rash
    • jolt accentuation (headache worse turning the head side to side): very sensitive, less specific
    • Kernig's sign (resists knee extension with the hip flexed) and Brudzinski's sign (neck flexion makes the hips flex): less sensitive, unreliable in coma and young children
  • Young children: irritability, poor feeding · drowsiness · vomiting · convulsions · bulging fontanelle (late - raised pressure) · rash
  • Risk factors: immunocompromise · chronic ear infection · diabetes · no spleen · alcohol use disorder · recent neurosurgery, CSF leak, shunt infection, penetrating head injury
  • Red flags for severity: breathing rate over 22 · systolic pressure under 100 · altered mental state
3. The approach to suspected meningitis

blocks.html:
• Why the CT first: with an abscess or mass, a lumbar puncture can make the brain herniate · also consider it where neurocysticercosis is endemic
  • Antibiotics delayed more than 6 hours after arrival in the emergency department → higher mortality (sources differ on order: the medwiki note lists cultures, then CT/lumbar puncture, then treatment; the upper-year notes start antibiotics straight after cultures - both say never wait for results - check the slides)
  • Lumbar puncture at L4/5, below the end of the cord · cell counts in tubes 1 and 4 (in case the tap itself causes some bleeding)

blocks.html: 4. Reading the cerebrospinal fluid

• Glucose ratio (CSF ÷ blood, drawn together): normal over 0.6 · bacterial low (sources differ: medwiki gives under 0.3; the upper-year notes say under 0.6 is abnormal, under 0.31 in 70% of bacterial cases, and under 0.4 in their table - check the slides)
  • Protein units for bacterial and viral are written as mg/mL in the upper-year table but mg/L for normal - check the slides
5. Empiric treatment in adults

rows: H. influenzae · N. meningitidis · penicillin-sensitive S. pneumoniae · S. aureus (methicillin-sensitive)
10 mg IV with the first antibiotic dose, then every 6 h for 4 days
↓ illness and death, most for S. pneumoniae

blocks.html: • Complications of bacterial meningitis: death · sepsis · seizures · raised pressure and brain swelling → herniation · cranial nerve palsies · hydrocephalus · vasculitis → stroke · cerebritis · abscess
6. Viral (aseptic) meningitis

• Aseptic = meningitis with no bacteria grown · often enteroviruses
  • Fever · headache · mild meningeal signs · light sensitivity · rash · uncomfortable but nowhere near as sick - often managed at home
  • Stop the antibiotics once the fluid is clearly viral · rest, fluids, pain relief · viral symptoms last 7-10 days, the headache can last weeks (warn the patient)
7. Herpes simplex encephalitis

• Encephalitis = infection of the brain tissue · mostly herpes simplex, which prefers the temporal lobes
  • Cortical features set it apart from meningitis: focal seizures · memory loss · aphasia · focal deficits (weakness, visual field loss) · behaviour change · fever and altered consciousness · rarely coma → herniation
    • fever + behaviour change + trouble understanding speech → think encephalitis
  • Diagnosis: CT first (often normal; may show subtle low density in the temporal lobe) · MRI: temporal lobe signal change · lumbar puncture: HSV PCR in the CSF is the confirmatory test · EEG · biopsy rarely
  • Treatment: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h (ideal body weight) for 14-21 days · start before the PCR result - earlier is better

lectures.name: Multidisciplinary Care in ALS
lectures.title: Multidisciplinary care in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ ALS = UMN and LMN signs together in two or more regions, with sensation and other non-motor systems spared. Riluzole buys only 2-3 months; BiPAP also extends life. Death is from respiratory failure or aspiration pneumonia, about 3 years from onset. Wheelchairs and splints belong to the OT; breathing and cough to the PT; swallowing and speech to the SLP.

blocks.html: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has no cure and only one weak drug, so the care is the team. The lecture turns on recognising the mixed upper and lower motor neuron picture, then on who does what as weakness spreads.
1. What ALS is

• Definition: a neurodegenerative disease with death of both upper motor neurons (UMN) and lower motor neurons (LMN)
    • motor neurons are lost in the cortex and in the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
  • How common: 2-3 per 100,000
  • Cause: 5-10% hereditary (autosomal dominant or recessive) · the rest sporadic, probably genes + environment + chance
  • Presents as: hand weakness · foot drop · slurred speech (dysarthria) · trouble swallowing (dysphagia) · shortness of breath (dyspnea) → weakness then spreads to most of the body
  • Course: average survival about 3 years from onset · death usually from respiratory muscle failure or aspiration pneumonia

blocks.alt: ALS symptoms by body region - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: ALS symptoms by region: bulbar (speech, saliva, swallowing), respiratory, upper body (hand weakness, dressing, handwriting) and lower body (tripping, stairs, weak feet)

blocks.html: 2. Diagnosis

• History: progressive, relatively isolated motor symptoms
  • Exam: LMN signs (atrophy, fasciculations) + UMN signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity) in at least two regions, without prominent non-motor involvement
  • Investigations only to rule out other explanations: nerve conduction studies · cerebrospinal fluid · MRI · metabolic tests
3. Treatment

• No cure
  • Riluzole is the only approved drug: a glutamate antagonist that reduces excitotoxicity · only extends life by 2-3 months
  • Bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) extends life once breathing becomes insufficient
  • Most important = managing symptoms, which needs a multidisciplinary team · follow up every 3-6 months
4. The multidisciplinary team

rows: Communication: dysarthria (spastic, flaccid or both) → strategies to be understood, or augmentative and alternative communication devices (picture board, eye gaze, voice amplifier) · Swallowing: assessment by modified barium swallow or fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing · safest textures (minced, puree, thickened liquids) · discusses feeding tubes

Breathing: shortness of breath and orthopnea (pacing, raising the head of the bed) · signs of chest infection · cough assistance (assisted cough, breath stacking, cough-assist machine) · suction · drooling (sialorrhea) · Limbs: range-of-motion exercises from active to passive as weakness grows · shoulder support to prevent subluxation · ankle-foot orthoses · fall safety
Independence in activities of daily living · home and vehicle modifications · equipment · splints and wheelchairs (OT, not PT) · work and leisure
First visit: psychosocial assessment (supports, work, income, insurance, wills and powers of attorney) · later: care needs, disability finances, adjustment and mood
Eating routine, swallowing limits, weight, bowels, skin · high-protein, high-calorie diet, texture changes · education about tube feeding
Explains the team, contact point between visits · coordinates meetings, follow-up and clinical trials

Confirms the diagnosis · drugs for drooling, spasticity, pain, constipation, depression, pseudobulbar affect · starts and monitors BiPAP with a respirologist · end-of-life discussions · trial recruitment

lectures.name: Brain Tumors
lectures.title: Brain tumours
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Progressive symptoms are the red flag for a brain tumour: a short history suggests a high-grade tumour, a long one a slow-growing tumour. Raised-ICP headache is worse lying down, in the morning and with straining; papilledema comes late. Enhancement on contrast MRI means a high-grade glioma; multiple ring-enhancing lesions with edema mean metastases. Metastases outnumber primaries; gliomas are the commonest primary, then meningioma, then CNS lymphoma. No steroids before biopsy in suspected lymphoma. Think before a lumbar puncture when a mass may be present.

blocks.html: A brain tumour shows itself by raised intracranial pressure, by a focal deficit, or by a change in the person - and the red flag tying them together is that the symptoms keep progressing. Metastases are more common than any primary tumour; among primaries, gliomas lead, and their grade sets the treatment.
1. Intracranial pressure (ICP)

• Normal: adults 5-15 mmHg (7-20 cm of water) · children 3-7 · infants 1.5-6 · abnormal in adults: 20 mmHg or more
  • Monro-Kellie doctrine: brain + cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) + blood + mass share a fixed skull → the brain first compensates by pushing out venous blood and CSF, then past a critical volume pressure rises steeply
  • Measuring it
    • lumbar puncture opening pressure · ⚠ a space-occupying lesion can herniate with a lumbar puncture → decide on a CT first (PUNISH)
    • invasive ICP monitor (with or without a drain): accurate, can drain CSF
  • Symptoms of raised ICP
    • lower level of consciousness (reticular activating system) · headache · vomiting (area postrema of the medulla) · Cushing's triad · papilledema, only late
    • herniation: third nerve palsy most common (fourth and sixth possible) · posterior cerebral artery compression and infarction · death
  • Raised-ICP headache: persistent, progressive, worse lying down, in the morning, and with coughing or straining (less venous return)
  • Causes: focal - tumour, hemorrhage, abscess, infarct · generalized - hydrocephalus, meningitis or encephalitis, cerebral edema

blocks.cap: Types of brain herniation: subfalcine (cingulate), central, uncal, tonsillar, transcalvarial and ascending

blocks.html: 2. How a brain tumour presents

• Headache
    • the brain itself is not pain-sensitive → headache comes when the tumour raises ICP or stretches the meninges (sources differ: the medwiki note calls headache often the first symptom, the upper-year notes say it is not common - check the slides)
    • suspicious if persistent, progressive, worse in the morning, with vomiting · can wake the patient (higher carbon dioxide during sleep swells the tumour)
  • Focal deficits by location: weakness · sensory loss · speech or swallowing trouble · gait or visual disturbance · begin insidiously and progress
  • Mental status change: apathy, withdrawal, personality change, confusion · often mistaken for depression or dementia
  • Seizures, especially focal
  • Duration hints at the tumour: weeks to months → highly malignant (glioblastoma) · months to years → benign or slow-growing
3. Approach and classification

• Most useful classification = primary vs secondary; also benign vs malignant, cell of origin, grade, molecular markers
  • "Malignant" means something different in the brain: these tumours rarely spread - they are called malignant because they recur locally

rows: Observe if no symptoms · biopsy then radiation when needed
Ring enhancement, necrotic centre, distorts the brain
2nd most common primary · arises from the meninges
Methotrexate-based chemotherapy ± radiation · surgery only for biopsy
Median over 3 years · worse if immunocompromised
Whole-brain radiation · resection if safe · stereotactic radiosurgery

blocks.html: 4. Gliomas

• Arise from glial cells · vary in histology, aggressiveness, response and prognosis
  • By cell of origin: astrocytoma (most common) · oligodendroglioma · ependymoma (rare)
  • By WHO grade (sources differ on the edition: the medwiki note says 2021, the upper-year notes 2016 - check the slides)

rows: Benign, often cured by surgery, usually a childhood tumour
Very fast, cell of origin no longer recognisable, necrosis and new vessels

blocks.html:
• Integrated diagnosis = histology + grade + molecular markers
    • IDH-mutant with 1p/19q co-deletion → better prognosis · IDH wild-type with 1p/19q intact → worse
    • astrocytoma is more aggressive than oligodendroglioma
  • Imaging: MRI over CT · always ask for contrast - enhancement usually means grade 3 or 4

blocks.alt: glioma grades on contrast MRI - low grade, anaplastic, glioblastoma - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Contrast MRI: a low-grade glioma does not enhance, an anaplastic oligodendroglioma enhances patchily, a glioblastoma shows ring enhancement around a necrotic centre

blocks.html: 5. Treating gliomas

• High grade (3-4): treat immediately · some low-grade need treatment, others can be watched
  • Gliomas (except grade I) are not surgically curable, but removing all visible tumour improves prognosis
  • Glioblastoma
    • maximal safe resection (biopsy if unsafe) → 15-30 radiation treatments over 3 weeks → temozolomide during and for 6-12 months after
    • median survival 10-12 months with radiation alone, 14-15 with temozolomide · 2-year survival 10% → 26%
  • Anaplastic (grade 3): treat like glioblastoma · oligodendrogliomas respond better to chemotherapy · median survival 3 years (astrocytoma), 7 years (oligodendroglioma)
  • Low grade: observe with serial MRI if no symptoms or only well-controlled seizures; biopsy deferred
    • treat when: new or progressive symptoms · clear radiologic progression (especially new enhancement) · patient preference · older patient or very large tumour
    • then biopsy or resect → post-operative radiation most common
6. Primary CNS lymphoma

• Arises from non-neural tissue but stays within the CNS · B-cell non-Hodgkin type in 90%
  • Risk: immunosuppression, HIV, but also immunocompetent older adults · incidence rising
  • Eye involvement 10-20%, leptomeningeal 40% → MRI, eye exam, lumbar puncture, HIV test
  • ⚠ Steroids can make it vanish before biopsy → avoid them until tissue is taken
7. Brain metastases

• Most common CNS tumours (likely underestimated) · 15% of people dying of cancer have them at autopsy
  • Usual primaries: lung (16% of brain metastases; small cell and adenocarcinoma) · breast · melanoma · renal cell
  • Rarely spread to brain: prostate, gastrointestinal, bladder, gynecologic → do not assume a brain lesion is a metastasis in these patients
  • Contrast MRI is the test of choice (a CT must have contrast) · biopsy still needed for a definite diagnosis
  • Treatment depends on clinical status and prognosis, alongside treating the primary

blocks.alt: multiple ring-enhancing brain metastases on contrast MRI - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Contrast MRI with several small ring-enhancing lesions: the typical look of brain metastases

blocks.html: 8. Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes

• Damage remote from the tumour, mostly immune-mediated · rare (0.01% of cancers)
  • The neurologic symptoms often come first, weeks to months before the cancer is found → search for a cancer, and repeat the search if the first is negative

rows: Small cell lung cancer, osteosclerotic myeloma

blocks.html: • Best treatment = treat the tumour

lectures.name: Pediatric Neurology
lectures.title: Pediatric neurology: the floppy infant
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The commonest cause of a floppy infant is not neurologic (sepsis, electrolytes, dehydration, heart disease) - and when it is neurologic, it is usually central. Weak + floppy + low reflexes = peripheral; strong + floppy + brisk reflexes + isolated axial floppiness = central. Central hypotonia turns into hypertonia by age 2-3. SMA is treatable and screened at birth. Congenital myotonic dystrophy: examine the mother.

blocks.html: A floppy (hypotonic) infant is usually sick rather than neurologically damaged - so rule out a non-neurologic cause first. If it is neurologic, decide central or peripheral: weakness with the floppiness points to the periphery, normal strength with brisk reflexes to the brain.
1. Tone and hypotonia

• Tone = resistance to passive movement around a joint
    • phasic tone: response to a rapid stretch, carried by the deep tendon reflexes
    • postural tone: response to low-intensity forces such as gravity
    • the two do not always go together
  • Hypotonia = low tone on passive stretch · not the same as weakness (a baby can be weak with good tone, or floppy with good strength)
  • Weakness + hypotonia almost always means a peripheral cause
  • In infants a central (brain) problem causes low tone, because the motor pathways are immature · it evolves to high tone by age 2-3, the pattern seen in adults
2. Sorting the causes

flowchart TD A["Floppy infant"] --> B{"Non-neurologic cause?
sepsis · electrolytes · dehydration
hypothyroidism · heart disease · failure to thrive"} B -->|Yes| C["MOST COMMON
treat the underlying illness"] B -->|No| D{"Weak? reflexes?"} D -->|"Normal strength · brisk reflexes
axial floppiness · seizures · poor cognition"| E["CENTRAL (most neurologic cases)
microarray · MRI · electroencephalogram (EEG)"] D -->|"Weak · reflexes low or absent
axial + limb floppiness · atrophy · normal cognition"| F["PERIPHERAL
creatine kinase · electromyography (EMG)
and nerve conduction studies
muscle biopsy · examine the mother"] F --> G["Localize: anterior horn cell · nerve
neuromuscular junction · muscle"]

blocks.html: • Most common overall: non-neurologic · when neurologic, most are central (80%)
3. History and exam

• History: pregnancy (reduced fetal movement, breech, delivery problems) · missed milestones, seizures · feeding, breathing or heart problems · family history
  • Exam: resting posture ("frog legs") · reflexes · tone · muscle bulk · joint contractures (arthrogryposis) · sensation and visual awareness · dysmorphic features · undescended testes (cryptorchidism)
  • Axial vs limb hypotonia
    • axial (posture muscles): curved back, poor head control, hips rolled in → isolated axial = central
    • appendicular (limbs): flexed arms, frog legs → axial + appendicular = peripheral
  • Traction response (pull-to-sit): normal baby flexes arms and lifts head · abnormal = head lag, no arm flexion
  • Vertical suspension: normal baby holds head up and flexes hips, knees, ankles · abnormal = head falls forward, legs dangle, slips through the hands
4. Central vs peripheral

rows: creatine kinase · EMG and nerve conduction · muscle biopsy · examine the mother

blocks.html: 5. Central causes

• Benign hypotonia of infancy: just lower tone, outgrown · later risk of joint dislocation
  • Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy: too little oxygen around birth (cord entanglement, placental insufficiency) → often permanent damage, can lead to cerebral palsy
  • Stroke, malformations, metabolic disorders
  • Chromosomal: Down syndrome · Prader-Willi syndrome
  • Spinal cord: rare (e.g. a congenitally narrow canal)
6. Peripheral causes, by site

rows: SMN gene, autosomal recessive, ~1 in 10,000 · the "ALS of childhood" · treatable (alter splicing of the SMN2 copy) → on Ontario newborn screening
Guillain-Barré syndrome (very rare in children) · Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (hypomyelinating forms)
Transient neonatal myasthenia · congenital myasthenic syndrome · infant botulism
Neonatal myasthenia = the mother's antibodies · botulism from spores → no honey for infants
Most common muscular dystrophy diagnosed in children · baby worse than the mother, who may not know she has it → examine the mother

blocks.html: • Both central and peripheral: leukodystrophies · storage diseases (Tay-Sachs disease, glycogen storage disease)
7. Cerebral palsy

• Cerebral palsy = disorders of movement and posture causing activity limitation, from a non-progressive disturbance of the developing fetal or infant brain
  • More common at lower gestational ages
  • Diagnosis usually by age 2 unless a clear insult is known · half of children with abnormal signs at 1 year outgrow them by 7

lectures.name: Non-Mendelian Genetics
lectures.title: Non-Mendelian genetics
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother, and heteroplasmy (a mix of normal and mutant copies, shared out at random) explains why the same mutation looks different in each tissue and worsens over time. Suspect mitochondrial disease when 2 or more high-energy organs are involved; lactate is raised. Anticipation = the repeat grows each generation, so onset is earlier and disease worse. Huntington's: CAG on chromosome 4, 40 or more repeats = full penetrance. Myotonic dystrophy: CTG in DMPK, cannot relax a grip.

blocks.html: Two ways inheritance breaks Mendel's rules: mitochondrial DNA comes only from the mother and is mixed unevenly in each cell, and repeat expansions grow from one generation to the next. That is why mitochondrial disease is variable and progressive, and why repeat disorders start earlier and hit harder in each generation (anticipation).
1. Mitochondria and their DNA

• Mitochondria are the cell's main energy source: the respiratory chain on the inner membrane (cristae) makes ATP by oxidative phosphorylation
  • Dual control: their proteins come from both nuclear and mitochondrial genes
  • Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA): circular, 37 genes, 1-10 copies per mitochondrion, in the matrix
  • Maternally inherited: the egg has many mitochondria; the sperm's are lost at fertilization
2. Heteroplasmy and why mitochondrial disease progresses

• Homoplasmy = every copy of mtDNA identical (healthy) · heteroplasmy = a mix of normal and mutant mtDNA
  • Point mutations are passed on by the mother · larger deletions and duplications are usually sporadic
  • At each cell division mitochondria are shared out at random, so the mutant load differs between cells and tissues · disease appears once a threshold is passed
  • Mitochondria also replicate in non-dividing cells (muscle, neurons) → mutant mtDNA accumulates → symptoms worsen over time
  • Mitochondrial depletion syndromes: nuclear gene mutations affecting mitochondrial nucleotide synthesis or mtDNA replication → too few working mitochondria

blocks.cap: Replication and random segregation of mutant mtDNA: from homoplasmy through heteroplasmy, with the mutant phenotype appearing once a threshold is crossed

blocks.html: 3. When to suspect mitochondrial disease

• High-energy tissues suffer first: brain, retina, skeletal muscle, heart
  • Consider it when 2 or more of these are present:

rows: hypotonia · ataxia · seizures · migraine · dementia · sensorineural hearing loss · intellectual disability
retinitis pigmentosa · optic neuropathy · nystagmus · eye muscle palsies
diabetes mellitus · diabetes insipidus · exocrine pancreatic insufficiency · short stature
Liver failure · intestinal pseudo-obstruction · renal tubular acidosis · Fanconi syndrome

blocks.html: 4. Investigations and treatment

• Raised lactate in blood and cerebrospinal fluid · MRI: basal ganglia changes, white-matter disease, atrophy, a lactate peak
  • Muscle biopsy with respiratory chain enzyme analysis · genetic panels (mtDNA and nuclear mitochondrial genes)
  • No effective treatment - supportive · a "mitochondrial cocktail" of cofactors (riboflavin, coenzyme Q10, thiamine) has little evidence
5. Trinucleotide repeat disorders and anticipation

• Anticipation = the repeat is unstable and tends to lengthen when passed on, so the disease starts earlier or is more severe in each generation
  • Penetrance rises with repeat length

rows: Loss of striatal neurons (indirect pathway) → too much movement
chorea · personality change, irritability, depression · cognitive decline to dementia · late: mute, rigid, dependent
All muscles, including the face: expressionless face, sunken cheeks, bilateral ptosis · heart and cognition can be affected · congenital form: respiratory failure, high infant death
Usually 30s-40s · survival 15-18 years · juvenile form (very large expansion): rigidity more than chorea, seizures, fast decline
Severity and age of onset track the repeat size
No cure · symptomatic drugs for movement and mood

blocks.html:
• Huntington's repeat length (CAG): 26 or fewer normal · 27-35 intermediate (not affected, but children may be at risk) · 36-39 reduced penetrance · 40 or more full penetrance
  • Testing: 70-80% of at-risk relatives choose not to be tested · presymptomatic testing only after genetic counselling (support, coping, reasons for testing) - hasty counselling can harm

blocks.cap: Huntington's CAG repeat length: 10-26 normal, 27-35 intermediate, 36-39 reduced penetrance, 40 or more full penetrance

blocks.html: 6. Variant of uncertain significance (VUS)
• An objective of this lecture, but not covered in the medwiki note or the upper-year notes - fill in from the slides

lectures.name: Movement Disorders
lectures.title: Movement disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Parkinson's tremor is at rest and asymmetric with slowness and rigidity; essential tremor is postural or action, symmetric, involves head and voice, and gets better with alcohol. Parkinsonism is a syndrome; ask about dopamine-blocking drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) before calling it Parkinson's disease. Levodopa works best on bradykinesia and must never be stopped suddenly. Vertical gaze palsy + early falls = PSP; autonomic failure = MSA.

blocks.html: Every movement disorder is the basal ganglia releasing too much movement (hyperkinetic) or too little (hypokinetic). The clinical work is telling a Parkinson's tremor from an essential tremor, and Parkinson's disease from the other causes of parkinsonism.
1. Hypokinetic vs hyperkinetic

• The basal ganglia select the movement you want and suppress the rest
    • direct pathway (dopamine D1) releases movement · indirect pathway (D2, via the subthalamic nucleus) suppresses competing movement
    • dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta boosts the direct pathway and damps the indirect one

rows: Too much inhibition of the thalamus → too little movement
Too little inhibition of the thalamus → too much movement
Ballismus: very quick, flinging · chorea: dance-like, fidgety · athetosis: slow, writhing · tremor · dystonia: sustained contraction, fixed posture · tics: an urge, held back for a while
Huntington's disease (indirect pathway lost) · too much levodopa (dyskinesia)

blocks.alt: basal ganglia indirect pathway - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The indirect pathway: cortex excites the caudate and putamen, which inhibit the external globus pallidus; the subthalamic nucleus drives the internal globus pallidus, which inhibits the thalamus. Dopamine acts through D1 and D2 receptors

blocks.html: 2. Parkinsonism vs Parkinson's disease

• Parkinsonism = a syndrome of tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability in any combination · Parkinson's disease is one cause
  • Other causes: basal ganglia lesions (stroke, bleed, tumour, infection) · drugs: antipsychotics, antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) · repeated head injury (chronic traumatic encephalopathy) · Parkinson-plus syndromes · toxins (carbon monoxide, cyanide)
3. Parkinson's disease

• Cause: Lewy bodies and loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta → loss of pigment (neuromelanin) without shrinkage · mostly sporadic
  • How common: about 1% over age 60
  • Features ("TRAP"), asymmetric
    • T - resting tremor, starts in one hand ("pill-rolling"), lessens with movement
    • R - rigidity: the same at any speed, increased by moving the other hand (augmentation)
    • A - akinesia and bradykinesia: trouble starting, slow finger tapping
    • P - postural instability
    • also: less blinking and facial expression · soft mumbling voice · less arm swing · stooped posture · small handwriting
  • Course: slow worsening · dyskinesia from treatment · depression, dementia · death usually from aspiration pneumonia

blocks.alt: substantia nigra pigment loss in Parkinson disease - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Midbrain: the normal substantia nigra contains pigmented cells (left); in Parkinson's disease the pigmented cells are lost (right)

blocks.html: 4. Treating Parkinson's disease

rows: Dopamine precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier · carbidopa stops it being broken down outside the brain

Most effective · best for bradykinesia and rigidity, variable for tremor · start low · ⚠ never stop suddenly (withdrawal) - keep giving it even when nothing by mouth · nausea, delirium · dyskinesia in 50% after 5 years
Slow dopamine breakdown in the brain

blocks.html: 5. Essential tremor vs Parkinson's tremor

rows: Holding a posture or moving (postural, action)
None if mild · beta-blockers, some antiseizure drugs · deep brain stimulation if refractory

blocks.html: 6. Parkinson-plus syndromes
• Parkinsonism plus other features · progress faster and shorten life more than Parkinson's disease

rows: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy - cannot follow a finger up and down; reflex eye movements are spared (so the lesion is above the nuclei)
Autonomic failure: orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, urinary incontinence
Early falls · neck stiffer than the limbs · no tremor, symmetric
Death in 4-7 years, often aspiration pneumonia

lectures.name: Monocular Vision Impairment
lectures.title: Monocular vision impairment
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Pale retina with a cherry-red spot and an RAPD is a central retinal artery occlusion - massage the eye, refer, and work it up like a stroke. Swollen disc with an RAPD: in an older patient with jaw claudication it is giant cell arteritis (steroids now); in a young woman it is optic neuritis (look for multiple sclerosis). Flashes, floaters and a curtain = retinal detachment. Glaucoma is optic nerve damage, not high pressure; it takes the periphery first and silently. Cataract = leading reversible cause of blindness; macular degeneration = leading irreversible cause.

blocks.html: Vision loss in one eye means the problem is in front of the optic chiasm; vision loss in both means behind it. Then sort by time course and pain: sudden loss is often an emergency (an "eye stroke", giant cell arteritis, a detached retina), slow loss is glaucoma, cataract or macular degeneration.
1. The approach

• History
    • one eye or both · all or part of the field
    • pain or no pain - the biggest narrowing question
    • time course: transient, persistent or progressive · "when was your vision last normal?"
    • medical history: diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, autoimmune disease · eye history: diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, eye surgery, contact lenses
  • Exam
    • visual acuity (against their baseline) · visual fields (blind spots)
    • pupils: swinging flashlight test for a RAPD = a retina or optic nerve lesion
    • red reflex: dull = something cloudy in the cornea, lens or vitreous
    • eye pressure (tonometry) · erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) and blood count if inflammation is possible · imaging if raised intracranial pressure is suspected
2. Causes of acute vision loss

rows: Sudden, painless · "a stroke of the eye"
Pale retina + cherry-red spot at the fovea · RAPD · other eye normal
Ocular massage (press and release with the heel of the hand for 5 minutes) to dislodge the embolus · refer · look for the source like a stroke (carotid stenosis, valve disease)

MRI to look for multiple sclerosis · high-dose IV steroids · refer · other causes: syphilis, Lyme, shingles, lupus

Swollen disc, cotton wool spots, flame hemorrhages · RAPD
New floaters, flashing lights, a grey curtain or peripheral field loss · acuity may be normal
Crinkled retina (hard to see) · dark moving spots in the red reflex
Painless · diabetes (proliferative retinopathy grows fragile vessels)
Lower the pressure now: oral acetazolamide or mannitol, topical beta-blocker, alpha-2 agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor · urgent referral

blocks.html: 3. Glaucoma

• Definition: a progressive, irreversible optic neuropathy (about 4% affected) · raised eye pressure is the main risk factor, not the definition - normal tension glaucoma damages the nerve at normal pressure
  • Presents as: nothing until late · peripheral field first → tunnel vision
  • The angle (where iris meets cornea) holds the trabecular meshwork that drains aqueous humour
    • open angle: the meshwork drains poorly · closed angle: the iris blocks the meshwork
  • Eye pressure (intraocular pressure, IOP): normal 10-21 mmHg · Goldmann applanation tonometry is the gold standard · Tono-Pen in the emergency department · air puff at the optometrist
  • Cup-to-disc ratio: normal about 0.3 · abnormal above 0.5 or asymmetric between the eyes
  • Referral: IOP 21 or more, or a suspicious disc · chronic open-angle = timely but not same-day, unless IOP is over 30 · acute angle closure = emergency
  • Treatment = lower the pressure, even from the normal range: drops, laser, surgery

blocks.cap: Optic disc in glaucoma: the cup grows from a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.2 (normal) to 0.7 and 0.99

blocks.html: 4. Cataract

• Cloudy or discoloured lens · leading cause of reversible blindness
  • Risk factors: age · genetics · trauma · steroids · metabolic disease, radiation, inflammation
  • Presents as: gradual loss of acuity · glare and halos around lights · "second sight" (near vision briefly improves) · hazy view on ophthalmoscopy · normal pressure
  • Treatment: surgery - the lens is replaced with an artificial one
5. Age-related macular degeneration
• Leading cause of irreversible blindness over 50 · central vision loss + distortion (metamorphopsia) · screen with an Amsler grid · refer

rows: Injections of anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) into the eye

lectures.name: Red Eye and Ocular Trauma
lectures.title: Red eye and ocular trauma
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Pain, photophobia or reduced vision turn a red eye from "probably conjunctivitis" into keratitis, uveitis or angle-closure glaucoma - and an urgent referral. Ciliary flush at the limbus means the cornea or iris is involved; diffuse redness with discharge means the conjunctiva. Abrasion stains but stays clear; an ulcer is hazy. Never give anaesthetic drops to take home, and never start steroid drops yourself. Suspected open globe: shield it and do not touch it.

blocks.html: Most red eyes are harmless; the job is to catch the few that threaten sight. Two questions do it: is it painful, and is the vision affected? A painless red eye with normal vision is usually the lids, the conjunctiva or a burst vessel; pain, photophobia or reduced vision means the cornea, the iris or the pressure, and an urgent referral.
1. Approach to the red eye

• History: onset (sudden: think subconjunctival hemorrhage) and timeline (intermittent: allergy) · pain, photophobia, vision change · discharge (how much, what kind) · itch · recent cold · sick contacts · contact lenses: do you swim, sleep or shower in them? · trauma or recent eye surgery (send back to the surgeon) · eye drops (preservatives irritate) · autoimmune disease · sexual history
  • Exam
    • visual acuity with glasses, one eye at a time
    • pupils (shape, size, light reaction) · eye movements · proptosis · lymph node in front of the ear · shingles rash
    • lids (evert to look for a foreign body) · discharge: purulent = bacterial; mucopurulent = viral possible; serous = many irritants
    • where the redness is: diffuse conjunctival hyperemia vs ciliary flush (a red ring at the limbus = cornea or uvea involved)
    • cornea for opacity · fluorescein under cobalt blue light (green = epithelium lost) · anterior chamber depth · blood (hyphema) or pus (hypopyon) · pressure if raised pressure is suspected
  • Red flags: blurred vision that does not clear with blinking · severe pain · photophobia · coloured halos · reduced acuity · ciliary flush · corneal opacity · pupil abnormality · raised pressure · proptosis · shallow anterior chamber
2. Red eye causes compared

Warm compresses and lid massage · stye: usually staphylococcus · refer for incision if not gone in 3-4 weeks
Lid turns in, lashes rub the cornea

blocks.html: 3. Ocular trauma

• Anatomy that matters (detail in 01 - Orbital Anatomy)
    • seven orbital bones · the maxilla is fractured most often · an orbital floor fracture numbs the cheek (infraorbital nerve)
    • the orbital septum divides preseptal (in front) from orbital (behind) infection
  • Exam: bony tenderness or step-off · air under the skin · lacerations (full thickness? tear duct?) · eye movements (cranial nerves III, IV, VI) · forehead and cheek sensation (V) · Seidel sign (fluorescein diluted by leaking aqueous = full-thickness wound)
  • Red flags → emergency ophthalmology: proptosis or sunken eye · foreign body protruding or inside the eye · deformed globe · no red reflex · relative afferent pupillary defect · peaked (tadpole) pupil · hypopyon · sudden loss of acuity · double vision · positive Seidel · 360° subconjunctival hemorrhage · dark tissue at the limbus (prolapsed iris)

rows: Pain (relieved by anaesthetic drops), tearing · rust ring if iron
Consider x-ray or CT · remove (irrigation, swab, fine needle) + antibiotic · refer if needed
Blood in the anterior chamber · pain, reduced vision, photophobia · all blood = "8-ball"
Shield · refer · limit activity · avoid blood thinners · steroid and pressure-lowering drops if needed
Blunt trauma or projectiles · ciliary flush, photophobia, cells
Bites, punches, handlebars · vision may be normal · medial: tearing (canaliculus cut)
Stab or poke · painful · may self-seal (pressure can look normal) · peaked pupil pointing to the wound · Seidel positive
Shield, do not touch - no lid eversion, no slit lamp · urgent surgery
