lectures.name: Pediatric Ophthalmology
lectures.title: Pediatric ophthalmology
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise - urgent referral. Amblyopia only happens in the critical period, so the earlier it is found and the good eye patched, the better. In the Bruckner test the brighter reflex is the turned eye; a dim or absent one means something cloudy. Concomitant squint (same angle in every direction) is the childhood kind; an angle that changes with gaze means a palsy or restriction. Constant turn at any age, or still intermittent after 3-4 months → refer.

blocks.html: A child's visual cortex only develops if each eye sends it a clear, aligned image during the early critical period - anything that blurs, blocks or misaligns one eye can leave it permanently weak (amblyopia). So the lecture is about catching that early: check acuity in each eye, look for a squint, and do the red reflex.
1. Amblyopia

• Amblyopia ("lazy eye") = reduced acuity without a detectable eye disease, from disrupted visual development · usually one eye
  • Why: in infancy the two eyes compete for the visual cortex · if one sees poorly, the other takes over, and in the extreme the weak eye loses its cortical representation · only in the critical period (first years) - the same blur in an adult does not cause amblyopia

rows: A large difference in focusing error between the eyes - the clearer eye wins
Something blocks or clouds the view: congenital cataract, corneal haze, ptosis
The brain suppresses the turned eye to avoid double vision

blocks.html:
• Test acuity in each eye separately - early detection is the point
    • newborns: red reflex · pupil reactions · fundus
    • under 2: cover one eye at a time - the baby fusses when the good eye is covered
    • 2 and up: picture or letter charts (HOTV, tumbling E)
  • Treatment: refer to pediatric ophthalmology promptly · patch the good eye · glasses, surgery · the earlier, the better

blocks.cap: Amblyopia: one eye sends a clear image and the other a blurred one, so the brain comes to favour the clear eye

blocks.html: 2. Strabismus

• Strabismus = the eyes point in different directions · esotropia (in) · exotropia (out) · hypertropia (up) · hypotropia (down)
  • Child: the brain suppresses the turned eye → strabismic amblyopia and permanent loss of depth perception (stereopsis) · Adult: double vision (diplopia)

rows: The same in every direction of gaze
Work normally, just not aimed together
One or more weak or tethered
Orbital trauma · Graves orbitopathy · nerve palsies

blocks.html:
• Tests
    • corneal light reflex: is the light's reflection in the same place on both corneas?
    • cover test: cover the good eye → the turned eye moves to take up fixation (useful after 6-7 months)
  • Treatment: patching, glasses or surgery · no evidence for eye exercises
  • Refer if: turn still occasional after 3-4 months · constant turn at any age · any nystagmus · abnormal red reflex, especially white
3. The red reflex

• Red reflex = light reflected back from the retina, red-orange (varies with fundus pigment) · the single most important test in pediatric ophthalmology: quick, non-invasive, no drops
  • Bruckner test: both eyes at once, in dim light, from far enough to see both pupils, child looking into the distance → compare the two
  • ⚠ Disease in both eyes can look symmetric and be missed

congenital cataract · corneal haze

also cataract · retinal disease"] D --> G["REFER"] E --> G F --> H["URGENT REFERRAL"]

blocks.html:
• Physiologic white reflex: light about 15° off-axis reflects from the optic nerve instead - common, but may still need an exam
  • Retinoblastoma: rare (about 1 in 180,000) · usually before age 4 · late diagnosis → 70% die; treated well → over 95% cured · 90% sporadic and one-sided; both eyes → essentially always familial · treated by removing the eye, chemotherapy, radiation, laser

lectures.name: In-Class - Approach to Seizures
lectures.title: In-class: approach to seizures
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Seizure over syncope: unconscious for more than a minute, eyes turned to one side, side-of-tongue biting, and confusion lasting minutes to hours; a faint lasts under a minute with only brief confusion. Focal slowing or spikes on EEG mean MRI. Valproate is the worst teratogen; levetiracetam and lamotrigine are the safer choices, with folic acid. Never stop antiseizure drugs because of pregnancy. A posterior shoulder dislocation should make you think of a seizure.

blocks.html: A case session built on the first-seizure approach (see the Week 14 approach to seizures chart for the workup and when to treat). What it adds: telling a seizure from a faint, reading the EEG report, and choosing a drug for a young woman.
1. Seizure or syncope?

• Differential of a brief loss of consciousness: syncope (low brain perfusion, cardiac or blood pressure) · seizure · psychogenic · sudden raised intracranial pressure (acute hydrocephalus) · brainstem transient ischemic attack (rare)

rows: None, tonic or clonic · may be asymmetric
Confusion for minutes to hours · possible Todd's paresis

blocks.html: • Movements: clonic = shaking · tonic = stiff · myoclonic = jerks
2. History clues

• Earlier seizures → more likely a seizure
  • Aura · asymmetric onset · deficit afterwards → focal seizure
  • Triggers (sleep loss, drugs or medications, head injury, illness, fever) → provoked vs unprovoked
  • Adults rarely present with a first generalized seizure - they present with focal ones · first generalized seizures are common in children
  • Adult first seizure: electrolytes and CT head now, EEG and MRI as an outpatient (full workup in the Week 14 chart)
3. EEG and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy

• Focal slowing or focal spikes on the electroencephalogram (EEG) = a focal lesion → MRI is required to look for cortical dysplasia, mesial temporal sclerosis, tumour or old infarct
  • Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: easily controlled - lifestyle (sleep, food, fluids) and low-dose drugs · a sleep-deprived EEG brings out the abnormality
4. Antiseizure drugs in young women

• Older antiseizure drugs weaken oral contraceptives → check interactions
  • Teratogens: always add folic acid · avoid the worst drugs in anyone who could become pregnant

rows: Valproate (highest malformation risk) · phenytoin · several drugs together

blocks.html: • ⚠ Do not stop antiseizure drugs for pregnancy: seizures risk fetal hypoxic injury, maternal status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP)
5. Complications of a seizure
• Posterior shoulder dislocation · injuries from falls · aspiration · status epilepticus (permanent brain injury) · SUDEP

lectures.name: The Dying Patient and MAiD
lectures.title: The dying patient and medical assistance in dying (MAiD)
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Stream 2 (natural death not reasonably foreseeable) adds a 90-day wait, an expert physician, and forbids the waiver of final consent. Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate. Advance care planning wishes are not consent; code status is not goals of care. The SDM order starts with a court guardian and a Power of Attorney for Personal Care, then spouse, child, parent, sibling. A conscientious objector must still make an effective referral.

blocks.html: Two questions run through the lecture: who gets to decide when the patient cannot (capacity → substitute decision maker), and, when the patient can and asks to die, are they eligible for MAiD and have the safeguards been met?
1. Capacity and the substitute decision maker

• Capacity has two parts
    • ① can understand the information relevant to the decision
    • ② can appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding (or not deciding)
    • specific to the decision (may be capable about meals but not about treatment) · can fluctuate over time
  • Substitute decision maker (SDM): gives or refuses consent for an incapable patient, taken in this order
    • ① court-appointed guardian · ② attorney under a Power of Attorney for Personal Care (not the one for property) · ③ representative appointed by the Consent and Capacity Board
    • ④ spouse or partner · ⑤ child over 16 · ⑥ parent · ⑦ sibling · ⑧ any other relative · ⑨ the Public Guardian and Trustee
2. Code status, goals of care, advance care planning

rows: Which resuscitation (if any) to give if the heart or breathing stops
Needs informed consent from the patient or SDM
A conversation about who the patient is, their values, and how those fit the clinical picture and treatment options
Code status is not the same as goals of care
Wishes voiced ahead of time to guide a future SDM
Wishes, not decisions - not "advance consent" (the future is speculation)

blocks.html: 3. Palliative care

• Definition: an approach that improves quality of life for patients and families facing life-threatening illness, by early identification, assessment and treatment of pain and other problems: physical, psychological, spiritual
    • also practical needs · dignity and comfort · bereavement counselling
    • most people would prefer to die at home, so it must be available in the community
  • Tools
    • Palliative Performance Scale (version 2): disease burden and progress toward end of life (the most used)
    • Edmonton Symptom Assessment System: screens for symptoms palliative care can manage
  • Routes in: the patient opts in · the physician judges treatment futile or too burdensome and suggests it · alongside active treatment for hard-to-control symptoms · after a severe irreversible disability (e.g. a stroke: choose comfort, no tube feeds or intravenous fluids)
4. Caring for the patient and family at the end

• Patient- and family-centred: speak to the patient even if comatose · look after the family's needs (rest, self-care) · answer questions honestly
  • Uncertainty: outcomes fall on a spectrum; a family told to expect the worst may be angry when the patient does better
  • Temporary improvement after stopping feeds, medications or fluids (hours to days) is common: reassure, use the time together, re-evaluate only if it lasts many days
  • Moral distress when a family's choice clashes with your values: "it is not my journey" · trust the SDM to choose as the patient would
  • Myths to answer
    • not starving to death: organs shut down together, no hunger or thirst · offer sips and tastes if wanted
    • turning the patient does not hasten death: it relieves pressure and lets staff check signs such as mottling (call the family)
    • patients often die as they lived (alone, or once the family has gathered) · give the family permission to step away
5. Medical assistance in dying (MAiD)

• Legal in Canada since 2016 · since 2021 two streams: ① natural death reasonably foreseeable · ② natural death not reasonably foreseeable
  • Eligibility: eligible for publicly funded health care (Ontario Health Insurance Plan, OHIP) · 18 or older and capable · a grievous and irremediable medical condition · a voluntary request, free of coercion · informed consent
  • Safeguards (both streams): written request witnessed by an independent person · two independent physicians confirm eligibility · consent again at the time of MAiD (stream 1 can waive this in advance)

blocks.html:
• Practical points
    • where: home, long-term care or hospital
    • organ donation is still possible afterwards (usually in hospital)
    • method: mostly intravenous benzodiazepine + high-dose propofol + a neuromuscular blocker, infused over 10 min, death within about 10 min · an oral lethal prescription is possible but rare
    • reporting: to the coroner (Ontario)
6. Conscientious objection

• A physician need not provide MAiD, but the patient keeps the right to access it, so the physician must:
    • act in a way that respects dignity and does not impede access
    • tell the patient directly and sensitively that the reason is personal, not clinical
    • make a timely effective referral, so delay does not harm the patient

lectures.name: Integration of Medicine and Neurology
lectures.title: Integration of medicine and neurology
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Stepwise multifocal strokes = cardioembolic until proven otherwise, and if it is endocarditis, no tPA - get two sets of blood cultures. Wernicke triad: ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, confusion - thiamine before glucose. B12 and copper deficiency both damage the posterior and lateral columns. Paraneoplastic symptoms often precede the cancer diagnosis.

blocks.html: The nervous system is often where a disease of another system shows itself. The lecture walks four systems in turn (cancer, breathing, nutrition, the heart) and asks for each: how does it reach the nerves, the cord or the brain?
1. Oncology: how cancer hurts the nervous system

rows: Spinal cord → myelopathy · nerve root → radiculopathy · peripheral nerve → mononeuropathy
Tumour grows into nerve, cord or brain
Metastases to the central nervous system, commonly from breast and lung
Antibodies made against the tumour attack nervous tissue
Limbic encephalitis · myasthenia gravis (acetylcholine receptor) · cerebellitis · dermatomyositis
Chemotherapy neuropathy · radiation encephalopathy · post-mastectomy pain syndrome
The drug releases the brake on T cells so they attack the tumour, and the body

blocks.html:
• Paraneoplastic syndromes (upper-year notes): rare, and the neurologic symptoms often come weeks to months before the cancer is found → recognise the syndrome and search for the tumour (repeat the search if the first is negative) · best treatment is to treat the tumour
  • Checkpoint inhibitor autoimmunity: talk to oncology about stopping the drug and/or giving steroids, knowing this may weaken the cancer treatment
2. Respirology: weak breathing from a nerve or muscle problem

• Lying down, the diaphragm does most of the work (it pushes the abdomen down) · upright, the intercostal muscles do most of it
  • Bilateral phrenic neuropathy → diaphragmatic weakness
  • Other neurological causes of diaphragm weakness: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) · Guillain-Barré syndrome
3. Nutrition: deficiencies and excesses

rows: Wernicke's encephalopathy: ataxia + eye-movement palsy (ophthalmoplegia) + confusion · dry beriberi = sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy · wet beriberi = heart failure, cardiomyopathy, edema (heart, not nerve)
Give thiamine before glucose in anyone whose nutrition is in doubt
Subacute combined degeneration (funicular myelosis): posterior and lateral columns of the cord · plus peripheral neuropathy and encephalopathy
The deficiency classically tied to neurological symptoms
After a long calorie deficit, refeed slowly and check electrolytes often (low sodium, calcium, magnesium, potassium)

blocks.html: 4. Cardiology: strokes in more than one territory

• Multifocal deficits arriving step by step are almost always cardioembolic strokes: one or several clots from the heart spray into several brain arteries
    • other multifocal causes: cerebral vasculitis · several tumours (metastases, primary central nervous system lymphoma) · several abscesses · demyelination (multiple sclerosis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis)
  • Cardiac sources: atrial fibrillation · endocarditis (recall FROM JANE) · cardiac tumours

flowchart TD A["Stepwise deficits in several brain territories"] --> B["Think cardioembolic stroke"] B --> C{"Signs of endocarditis?
the FROM JANE features"} C -->|"No"| D["Look for atrial fibrillation or a cardiac tumour
(upper-year notes: echocardiogram, heart-rhythm monitoring)"] C -->|"Yes"| E["Do NOT give tPA"] E --> F["Two sets of blood cultures
Staph aureus #1 · streptococci · enterococci · HACEK"]

blocks.html:
• Endocarditis + stroke: no clot-busting drug (tissue plasminogen activator, tPA) · upper-year notes: listen to the heart before giving tPA, because of the risk of infected (mycotic) aneurysms
  • Staphylococcus aureus is the #1 cause of endocarditis (31%)

lectures.name: Autopsy Review
lectures.title: Autopsy review
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A medicolegal autopsy falls under the Coroner's Act, so the family cannot refuse it; a hospital autopsy needs informed authorization from the next of kin, who may restrict it. Part I runs backwards: each line is caused by the one below it; Part II holds contributors outside the chain. Never write a mechanism ("cardiac arrest", "multisystem organ failure", "sepsis") as the cause. Sudden and unexpected deaths are signed by the coroner, expected natural ones by the doctor.

blocks.html: Two questions decide everything about a death: who has the authority (the family, or the coroner under the Coroner's Act), and what actually caused it, written as a chain of diseases, not as the way the body stopped.
1. Two kinds of autopsy

rows: Natural (family request, teaching, quality assurance, genetics, research)
The Coroner's Act - the family cannot refuse

blocks.html: 2. The hospital autopsy

• Informed authorization: from the next of kin or estate trustee, who can limit it
    • the pathologist may wish to keep organs for further study (most often brain and heart); the family can refuse
  • What it is for
    • diagnose disease, its extent, and the effect of treatment
    • check the accuracy of clinical tests · settle unanswered clinical questions · look for a suspected genetic disease (findings that matter to living relatives)
    • research and teaching · helps the family's grief · informs the death certificate
  • Steps: ① medical history (records, ambulance calls, clinicians) → ② external exam (nutrition, scars, tattoos) → ③ internal exam (Y-shaped incision, organs examined and weighed, brain) → ④ extra studies (histology, genetic testing, blood) → ⑤ synthesis of an opinion in the context of the case
3. The death certificate

• A permanent record of what disease, injury or event led to the death · used for statistics, research, surveillance, funding and legal records
  • Contains identification · cause of death · manner of death · autopsy results if available · (a stillbirth uses a different form)
  • Who signs: sudden and unexpected → coroner or medical examiner · expected natural → doctor or certain nurses
4. Cause of death: the WHO format

• Cause of death = the disease or injury that ended life
  • Part I: the chain of events, working backwards from the final condition - each line is caused by the line below it (1a ← 1b ← 1c, the last being the underlying cause)
  • Part II: other conditions that contributed but are not in the chain (often risk factors)

• Be specific
    • infection: the disease and/or organism, and the site (COVID-19 pneumonia · Haemophilus influenzae meningoencephalitis)
    • cancer: site of origin, site of spread, and type (pulmonary metastasis of colonic adenocarcinoma)
  • Leave out the mechanism of death - it adds nothing about the cause: cardiac arrest · arrhythmia · exsanguination · respiratory arrest · multisystem organ failure · sepsis

lectures.name: Hearing Loss
lectures.title: Hearing loss
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Weber lateralizes to the bad ear in a conductive loss and to the good ear in a sensorineural loss; Rinne (bone louder than air) confirms the conductive side. Sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency - steroids within 10 days and an MRI. Conductive loss leaves an air-bone gap; sensorineural does not. Presbycusis takes the high pitches; noise makes a 4,000 Hz notch. One-sided sensorineural loss with tinnitus and imbalance: think vestibular schwannoma.

blocks.html: Every hearing-loss question turns on one split: is sound failing to reach the inner ear (conductive), or is the inner ear or its nerve failing (sensorineural)? The tuning forks make that split at the bedside, and a sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency where a sudden conductive one is not.
1. Sound and the ear

• Sound: frequency 20-20,000 hertz (Hz) · loudness in decibels (dB), a log scale · we hear best at 2,000-4,000 Hz, the range of speech
  • Outer ear: auricle + a 3 cm canal that protects the drum and resonates at 2,000-4,000 Hz
  • Middle ear: air-filled · tympanic membrane · ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) turn air vibration into force that can move fluid at the oval window · Eustachian tube equalizes pressure with the pharynx
  • Inner ear: the cochlea, three fluid channels (scala vestibuli and tympani: perilymph · scala media: potassium-rich endolymph)
    • organ of Corti on the basilar membrane: inner hair cells transduce, outer hair cells amplify
    • oval window pushed in by the stapes · round window bulges out to let the fluid move
    • tonotopic: base is stiff → high pitch · apex is floppy → low pitch
    • pathway: brainstem → medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus → superior temporal gyrus
2. History and the tuning forks

• History: loudness or clarity · duration · sudden or gradual onset · speed of progression · one or both ears · ear pain · discharge · fullness · tinnitus · vertigo · facial and trigeminal symptoms
  • Exam: otoscopy · pneumatic otoscopy shows whether the drum moves
  • Tuning forks (512 Hz): always do both - the Weber alone cannot tell a conductive loss in one ear from a sensorineural loss in the other

flowchart TD A["Hearing loss in one ear"] --> B["Weber: fork on the midline of the head
Where is it louder?"] B -->|"Midline"| C["Normal: no one-sided loss"] B -->|"Louder in the BAD ear"| D["Rinne in the bad ear:
fork on mastoid, then beside the ear"] B -->|"Louder in the GOOD ear"| E["Rinne in the bad ear"] D -->|"Bone louder than air"| F["CONDUCTIVE loss in the bad ear
not urgent, even if sudden"] E -->|"Air louder than bone, as normal"| G["SENSORINEURAL loss in the bad ear"] G --> H{"Came on over less than 3 days?"} H -->|"Yes"| I["SUDDEN SENSORINEURAL LOSS: EMERGENCY
ear, nose and throat referral · audiogram · MRI
steroids by mouth or into the ear, within 10 days"] H -->|"No"| J["Audiogram · look for the cause"]

blocks.cap: Weber test: louder in the affected ear with a conductive loss, in the better ear with a sensorineural loss
Rinne test: air conduction normally beats bone; bone beats air in a conductive loss

blocks.html: 3. Investigations

• Audiogram (nearly everyone): hearing level in dB against frequency
    • air conduction (through drum and ossicles): O right, X left · bone conduction (straight to the cochlea): < right, > left
    • conductive: bone normal, air worse (an air-bone gap) · sensorineural: bone and air equally worse · mixed: both
  • Auditory brainstem response: for newborns, and suspected malingering
  • Acoustic reflex (stapedius, facial nerve): absent with a conductive loss, a severe sensorineural loss, a vestibulocochlear nerve lesion on the side receiving sound, or a facial nerve lesion on the side measured
  • Tympanometry (drum compliance against pressure): high peak = floppy drum (ossicle disruption, thin healed drum) · shallow peak = stiff (otosclerosis) · flat = drum not moving (perforation, middle ear fluid) · shifted peak = retracted drum (Eustachian tube dysfunction)
  • Imaging: CT for bone and ossicles · MRI for soft tissue (tumours)

blocks.cap: Audiogram: air conduction as O (right) and X (left), bone conduction as < and >; here both ears lose the high pitches

blocks.html: 4. Conductive vs sensorineural

rows: Outer or middle ear: sound blocked before the cochlea
Hair cells, the auditory nerve, or the brain
Cannot be repaired: hearing aid or cochlear implant
Wax · otitis externa · otitis media and effusion · perforation · otosclerosis · longitudinal temporal bone fracture
Presbycusis · noise · ototoxic drugs · vestibular schwannoma · Ménière's · transverse temporal bone fracture · congenital

blocks.html: 5. Conductive causes

• Outer ear
    • Impacted wax (very common): irrigate with room-temperature water aimed at the top of the canal (cold or hot water causes a caloric response; too deep risks perforation)
    • foreign body (children) · a hearing-aid battery in the ear is an emergency
    • exostoses: benign bony bumps from childhood cold-water exposure, remove only if troublesome
    • Bacterial otitis externa (swimmer's ear): sore, swollen canal · Pseudomonas, Staph aureus, E. coli · debride, acidify only if the drum is intact, antibiotic drops ± a wick
    • Fungal otitis externa: itch more than pain · Aspergillus (black spores) or Candida (white) · often after antibiotic drops · recurrent → think diabetes · clean, antifungal drops
    • chronic otitis externa (over 3 months, often cotton swabs): steroid drops, or excision and skin graft
  • Middle ear
    • Acute otitis media: pus behind a bulging, cloudy drum, after a cold · pain, fever, irritability · Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae · amoxicillin
    • Otitis media with effusion: fluid without infection (Eustachian tube dysfunction) · fluid in both ears for 3+ months → hearing test (speech and development) · tympanostomy tubes to drain it
    • adhesive otitis media: drum scarred onto the middle ear → ossicle erosion, cholesteatoma
    • Perforation: ~80% heal alone · keep dry · tympanoplasty if not
    • Otosclerosis: abnormal bone fixes the stapes · autosomal dominant, variable penetrance · conductive or mixed loss · stapedectomy
    • Longitudinal temporal bone fracture (80%, blow to the side): perforation, blood behind the drum, ossicle dislocation
6. Sensorineural causes

• Presbycusis: the most common · high pitches first, more in men · 30% over 65, 50% over 75 · progressive, irreversible
  • Noise-induced: over 85 dB for an 8-hour shift is the workplace limit · notch at 4,000 Hz on the audiogram · prevention = hearing protection
  • Ototoxic drugs: aminoglycosides · platinum chemotherapy (cisplatin, carboplatin) and vincristine · loop diuretics · ASA (acetylsalicylic acid) and quinine (reversible) · macrolides (temporary)
  • Sudden sensorineural loss: onset under 3 days, ± tinnitus, fullness, vertigo · mostly idiopathic · MRI because ~2% are an acoustic neuroma · steroids within 10 days · 60-80% recover
  • Transverse temporal bone fracture (20%, blow front-to-back): damages the vestibulocochlear nerve and the inner ear · worse prognosis
  • Vestibular schwannoma ("acoustic neuroma"): benign, slow, the commonest cerebellopontine angle mass · one-sided sensorineural loss, tinnitus, imbalance, facial and trigeminal symptoms · bilateral → neurofibromatosis type II · watch, radiation or surgery
  • Congenital: two-thirds non-syndromic (genetic), one-third syndromic
7. Treatment

• Conductive: treat the cause (medicine or surgery: tympanoplasty, ossicle repair, stapedectomy) · air-conduction hearing aids · bone-conduction aids when air aids cannot work (e.g. a closed canal): bone-anchored (implanted) or a bone-conduction implant under the skin
  • Sensorineural: damage cannot be repaired · hearing aids raise volume but may not fix clarity · cochlear implant stimulates the auditory nerve directly, bypassing outer and middle ear, using the cochlea's tonotopic map (needs a working nerve)

lectures.name: Vertigo
lectures.title: Vertigo
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Vertigo plus another brainstem sign (double vision, crossed sensory loss) is central until proven otherwise; vertigo alone points to the ear. Attack length and hearing name the peripheral cause: seconds = BPPV, minutes to hours with hearing loss = Ménière's, days without hearing loss = vestibular neuritis, with hearing loss = labyrinthitis. COWS: cold opposite, warm same (fast phase). BPPV: Dix-Hallpike to diagnose, Epley to cure. Sound-induced vertigo with autophony = superior canal dehiscence.

blocks.html: "Dizzy" can mean anything, so the history does the work: first, is it true vertigo (an illusion of spinning)? Then is it peripheral (inner ear or nerve) or central (brainstem)? Then how long does each attack last, and is hearing affected? That last pair names most peripheral causes.
1. Vestibular physiology

• The vestibular apparatus sits beside the cochlea, shares the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII), and uses the same hair cells in potassium-rich endolymph
  • Two kinds of sensor

rows: Endolymph lags behind (inertia) and bends the cupula
Ear stones (otoconia) weigh down a gel membrane that bends the hair cells
Three canals at right angles · each paired with one on the other side
One horizontal, one vertical (sources differ on which is which - check the slides)

blocks.html:
• Resting firing is always on, so a hair cell can signal both ways (bend toward → more firing, away → less)
  • The brain reads the difference between the paired canals: turning the head right raises one side and lowers the other
  • Acute loss of one side = a false difference → vertigo, nystagmus, ataxia, nausea and vomiting
2. Nystagmus and the vestibular reflexes

• Nystagmus: rhythmic to-and-fro eye movement, named by its fast phase (slow phase = vestibular drift, fast phase = reset)
    • physiological: rotation, caloric, optokinetic (watching scenery from a car), end-gaze · pathological: spontaneous (fixed direction), positional
  • Vestibulo-ocular reflex: holds the image still on the retina during head movement, faster than vision can
  • Caloric test (patient lying down): COWS = Cold Opposite, Warm Same (direction of the fast phase)
    • cold water mimics a head turn away (less firing) → fast phase to the opposite side · warm mimics a turn toward → fast phase to the same side
    • in coma: tests the brainstem · no movement = brainstem lesion · only one eye moves = medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion (conjugate gaze lost)

blocks.alt: caloric test warm vs cold irrigation - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Caloric test: warm water raises endolymph and firing in that horizontal canal; cold water lowers it

blocks.html: 3. Balance and the dizzy patient

• Balance needs 2 of 3 inputs: ① vestibular ② vision ③ proprioception · integrated centrally by the cerebellum → eye muscles and postural muscles
  • Vertigo = an illusion of rotary movement · "dizziness" may instead be lightheadedness or unsteadiness
  • History is everything (anxiety often adds to it) · exam: look for nystagmus and ataxia

rows: Hearing symptoms · vagal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, sweating) · worse with head movement
Loss of consciousness · cardiac or neurological features

Organic: presyncope and syncope, arrhythmia, orthostatic hypotension, hyperventilation, anemia, peripheral neuropathy, poor vision, drugs · psychiatric: depression, anxiety, panic disorder, phobic dizziness, somatization

blocks.html: 4. Peripheral vs central vertigo

rows: Inner ear (end organ) or the vestibular nerve
Vertigo on its own, ± hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness
Vertigo + another brainstem sign: double vision · crossed sensory loss (face one side, body the other) · ataxic hemiparesis
Neuritis or labyrinthitis: fixed direction, beating away from the affected ear
BPPV · Ménière's · vestibular neuritis · labyrinthitis · superior canal dehiscence
Brainstem stroke (the upper-year case: a 54-year-old with vertigo, nausea and a fall)

blocks.html: • The sources give no bedside exam set for telling these apart beyond the history and neurological exam - check the slides
5. Time course × hearing: naming the peripheral cause
6. The vertigo syndromes

rows: Loose otoconia drift into a canal, usually the posterior (lowest) · idiopathic or head trauma
Under 1 min, triggered by looking up or rolling over in bed
Dix-Hallpike maneuver shows upbeat rotary nystagmus toward the lower ear · Epley maneuver: ~80% cured after one, ~95% after three
Hole in the bone over the superior canal = a third window into the inner ear
Brief, set off by loud sound or pressure
Conductive loss · hears own voice, footsteps, eye movements
Audiometry + temporal bone CT · avoid triggers, or surgery
Excess endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops) · secondary causes = Ménière's syndrome (syphilis, trauma, labyrinthitis)
Low salt, lifestyle (caffeine), vestibular suppressants in attacks, diuretics, betahistine, steroids into the ear (controls ~80%) · refractory: gentamicin into the ear, nerve section, labyrinthectomy
Vestibular nerve only, often after a cold (viral)
Antiemetics and vestibular sedatives · oral steroids if early (within 72 h) · antivirals do not help
